articles.title: Iran could move shadow war in a dangerous direction, experts warn on back of two possible terror attacks
articles.summary: Two suspected plots near RAF Fairford and aboard a FlyDubai flight raise questions about Iran's covert attacks against the United States and Israel.
articles.body:
Concerns are rising that Iran may increase covert attacks following the FlyDubai stabbing and suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford.

Counterterrorism police have arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, but investigations have not publicly established Iranian government involvement in the attacks.

Experts caution that the recent attacks may not necessarily indicate a shift in Iran's war strategy, as Tehran has historically used proxies and intermediaries to carry out operations with deniability.

The FlyDubai stabbing is contributing to concerns that Iran could increase covert and deniable attacks as the conflict with the United States and Israel drags on.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, meanwhile, said there are "strong indications" Iran played a role in a suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford, the British air base used by U.S. forces during operations against Iran. Counterterrorism police have since arrested a dual U.K.-Iranian national on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

The two suspected attacks are raising questions over whether Iran's war strategy is shifting, but experts caution not to treat the incidents as equally indicative of Iranian involvement — or evidence yet that Tehran has changed its tactics.

President Donald Trump said early information he has received points to a possible Iranian connection to the attack aboard an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight, where a co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft with more than 180 people aboard.

The United Arab Emirates and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have described the FlyDubai incident as terrorism, but UAE authorities have not publicly attributed the attack to Iran. Neither investigation has publicly established that the Iranian government directed the attacks, and Iran has denied involvement in the Fairford case .

Daniel Byman, director of the Warfare, Irregular Threats and Terrorism Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the Fairford case fits more closely with Iran's recent use of hired operatives and other intermediaries.

"The attack on the airbase in the United Kingdom does fit more recent patterns," Byman told Fox News Digital, while stressing how much remains unknown about the investigation.

The FlyDubai attack would be a more significant departure.

"That is quite different, and that is something that Iran in the past, at least we haven't seen Iran do," Byman said. "It is plausible to me that Iran is involved, but that seems like much more of a stretch based on Iran's traditional way of operating."

But the uncertainty surrounding the attacks also illustrates part of the appeal of the broader strategy Iran has spent decades developing: using proxies, covert operatives, criminal networks and other intermediaries to threaten adversaries far beyond its borders while making Tehran's own role more difficult to establish.

Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury and FBI counterterrorism official who now directs the Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence at the Washington Institute, said Iran has increasingly sought to put more distance between itself and the people carrying out overseas operations.

"Typically Iran does not admit that it's involved in these types of attacks because it wants reasonable deniability," Levitt said.

"There are several advantages for Iran to using terrorism," Byman said. "One is that there is often a degree of deniability."

"Terrorism gives Iran a lot more reach," he added. Levitt, however, put the distinction with conventional warfare more bluntly.

"If Iran shoots a drone or a missile at you, you know where it came from and you know where to shoot back," he said. "But if Iran uses proxies, and recruits people and does things in a covert manner, it might not be so easy to point a finger back at Iran or to know exactly who did it."

That capability matters in part because Iran does not have the conventional military strength to match the United States and its allies directly, Levitt said.

"They just don't have the capability to fight soldier to soldier, airplane to airplane in an all-out kinetic war, but they're extremely effective at asymmetric warfare, at covert terrorist activity, if that's what this proves to be," he said.

Recent U.S. prosecutions have shown how far that playbook can extend. Federal cases have accused Iranian operatives of seeking to recruit hitmen to kill U.S. officials and using Eastern European organized crime figures in a murder-for-hire plot targeting Iranian-American journalist and dissident Masih Alinejad in New York.

Those operations relied on the same basic advantage: Tehran could pursue targets overseas without launching a conventional attack that immediately identified Iran as the aggressor.

The question now is whether the current conflict gives Iran reason to push that strategy further.

Levitt said Tehran could pursue overseas plots in an effort to pressure Western governments to end the conflict by demonstrating that Iran can impose costs far beyond the conventional battlefield.

And if Fairford and FlyDubai are ultimately tied to Tehran, he said, they would stand out because they involve harder targets and potentially more ambitious tactics than the assassinations, kidnappings, shootings and smaller-scale bombings Iran has more commonly pursued overseas.

"Perhaps this is the new normal, and Iran wants to demonstrate that it can exact a higher cost," Levitt said.

Byman, however, pointed to several reasons Tehran could exercise restraint.

Iran already has other ways to pressure Washington and its allies, while a terrorist attack against Americans could backfire by uniting U.S. public opinion behind further escalation against Tehran, he said. U.S. and Israeli strikes against senior Iranian intelligence and security officials may also have disrupted some of the networks Tehran would need for overseas operations.

"If Iran wants to go further, then terrorism does become more of an option," Byman said.

articles.title: Mumbai airport crackdown: Afghan, Bangladeshi, Nepalese nationals held with Indian passports
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Immigration officials at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport intercepted three foreign nationals — from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and
articles.body: MUMBAI: Immigration officials at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport intercepted three foreign nationals — from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Nepal — on October 3 and 4 for allegedly obtaining Indian passports using forged documents and false information.Sahar police said the passports were issued in Mumbai and Kolkata, allegedly with the help of agents. Police are investigating the network involved. All three men were arrested.Bangladeshi national Robindra Mondal, 48, was handed over to police on October 3 after allegedly attempting to travel to Abu Dhabi on an Indian passport. He was scheduled to board Etihad flight EY207 before travelling onward to Paris.Immigration records allegedly linked him to two Bangladeshi passports issued in Dhaka under the name Rabindra Mondol, listing his birthplace as Munshiganj, Bangladesh, and his date of birth as June 12, 1978. Officials said Mondal admitted that he had entered India illegally and later obtained Aadhaar and PAN cards as well as an Indian passport.He allegedly secured Indian passport AP-472113 from Kolkata on May 11, 2026, using false details.Nepalese national Deepak Giri, 40, who arrived from Kathmandu on IndiGo flight 6E1158 on October 3, was questioned after immigration checks showed frequent travel to Kathmandu and he failed to provide satisfactory information.Records showed that Giri was born in Ramechhap, Nepal, held Nepalese citizenship and married a Nepalese citizen in Manthali Municipality on December 14, 2022. His parents had moved to Mumbai in 1980.Police said Giri allegedly obtained an Indian passport from Mumbai on September 16, 2021, using false or incorrect information.Afghan national Taza Khan Zurmati was intercepted on October 4 while allegedly attempting to fly to Dubai as Ibrahim Khan on IndiGo flight 6E-1451. Immigration officials became suspicious after finding Afghan visa stickers in his Indian passport.A biometric search reportedly found two Afghan passports in the names of Taza Khan Zurmati and Taza Khan. Records showed that he entered India on a medical attendant visa on May 19, 2016, returned to Afghanistan on October 15 that year, and re-entered India for treatment on September 5, 2017.Police said Zurmati overstayed after his visa expired and later obtained Aadhaar, PAN and voter ID cards. articles.title: British Airways flight to Chicago drops 28,000 feet, returns to London
articles.summary: About 30 minutes into its journey, the aircraft dropped from 36,000 feet to 9,000 feet in around seven minutes, according to flight-tracking website FlightAw...
articles.body:
LONDON — A British Airways passenger jet flying from London to Chicago descended 28,000 feet in just seven minutes after declaring an emergency due to an unspecified "technical issue," the airline said Monday.

The Boeing 777 took off at 12:15 p.m. local time (7:15 a.m. ET) but started descending just 30 minutes later while flying over Ireland, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware .

The plane turned around and spent around four hours zigzagging over the Bristol Channel, a waterway to the west of England, before landing back at London Heathrow Airport at 5 p.m. local time (noon ET).

"The aircraft landed safely after our highly-trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue," British Airways said in an emailed statement. "Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible."

Heathrow did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Passengers will likely be put up in hotels by the airline until another flight can be arranged, as stipulated by the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority.

Britain's National Air Traffic Service (NATS) came under scrutiny last month after two technical problems in the space of two weeks caused major delays at several U.K. airports and hundreds of flights were canceled.

NATS blamed software issues for the delays.

Britain's Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation had been "deeply frustrating" for passengers.

With 84.5 million passengers last year, Heathrow ranked seventh in the table of the world's busiest airports, according to data published by Airports Council International.

Travel from Heathrow was severely disrupted in March last year when a massive fire at an electricity substation caused a predawn power outage at the global transport hub.

The closure affected more than 1,300 flights and 200,000 passengers.

After investigating 600 items of evidence related to the substation, the National Energy System Operator ruled out suspicious activity in a report saying a preventable moisture fault caused the fire, leaving almost 70,000 homes without power.

articles.title: 'If SIR excludes citizens from voterslist, what is its purpose?': Bombay high court to EC
articles.summary: Bombay High Court questions Election Commission over Goa voter deletions during SIR, says citizens face “Catch-22” as Form 8 rejected and Form 6 risks false declaration.
articles.body: PANAJI: Bombay high court Monday grilled Election Commission over how Paresh Salgaonkar and his family of five were deleted from the Goa electoral rolls despite being Indian citizens and submitting Form 8 for change of address.“…the Election Commission has a constitutional obligation to ensure that only persons who are citizens are on the rolls. If by this process (special intensive revision or SIR), citizens are excluded, then what is the purpose of this mandate,” the two-judge bench of Justices Valmiki Menezes and Amit Jamsandekar asked EC.The court told EC that the entire exercise of SIR was to find out whether the voter is an Indian citizen or not.“The basis of SIR is not to see whether the voter is present in a particular place or not, but to find out whether the voter is an Indian citizen or not. This seems to be the reason why there is an SIR,” the court said.Reminding EC of Rule 21 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, the court said, “everything must be seen qua the existing roll and not draft roll, otherwise a voter has absolutely no way out of this”; the judges said, adding EC has put the voter “in a Catch-22 situation”.The court questioned EC on whether it issued notices to the family before deleting their names from the rolls.Gaurish Agni, counsel representing the Election Commission, said notices were published on notice boards at every level because the voters’ fresh details may not be available with the commission.Agni said, according to the guidelines, Form 8 could not have been processed for those whose names stood deleted from the draft rolls as they hadn’t filled in enumeration forms. He said Salgaonkar could have filled Form 6 because he’s a new voter in a new part and because the SIR treats it as though the roll is starting completely afresh.“Form 8 is an objection to the draft roll from that place. It is to correct your draft roll and include the voter’s name. Form 8 is precisely that,” the bench said, adding Form 6 is for declaring that someone’s name is missing from the place where the voter resides, and he/she should be added to the rolls.“If he gives you Form 6, it’s a false declaration. If he gives you Form 8 (for change of address), you do not accept it but ask him to give the enumeration form. There are no enumeration forms in the history of this country,” the judges said.The court asked how a person who has shifted from one part to another and who was already on the rolls could be asked to give a Form 6 declaration in the prefilled enumeration form.“The declarations are such that the voter has to declare in a prefilled form to include the person in that same place, while the person is not residing in that place. How will a person make such a declaration when he knows his name is in another place? The moment he makes this declaration, he’s open to prosecution. This is a false statement…” the bench said.“No voter is going to sign this. No voter should sign this. We are saying they should not sign this. How can he apply for inclusion in this place if he doesn’t reside there?” the court said and asked EC to submit the enumeration form and annexures to forms.The bench will continue the hearing of the matter Tuesday.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Goa | Silver Rate in Goa | Bank Holidays in Goa | Public Holidays in Goa | Petrol Price in GoaStay updated with the latest Goa news. articles.title: 19km roads for end-point connectivity for Hinjewadi Metro
articles.summary: Pune plans 19.2 km of last-mile connectivity roads for Hinjewadi Metro, to be built by MIDC and PMRDA near eight stations, by December.
articles.body: Pune: The govt is planning to develop a total of 19.2 km of roads for last-mile connectivity for commuters using the upcoming Hinjewadi metro. The roads will be initially developed at eight out of the 12 Metro stations that will be operational in the first leg.The stations include Megapolis circle, Quadron circle, Dohler station, Infosys phase 2 station, Wipro Technologies station, Pall India station, Shivaji Chowk station and Hinjewadi station.Maharashtra Industrial Development Authority (MIDC) and Pune Metropolitan Region Development Authority (PMRDA) will jointly develop the last-mile connectivity roads. The construction work is expected to be completed by Dec. The carriageways will be 12-30 m wide and will have lengths of 0.5-1.5 km. “We have identified residential and office clusters within 500 m of the Metro stations within which these roads will be developed along with footpaths and a bicycle track,” Abhijit Chaudhari, commissioner, PMRDA, said in a meeting held in Sept detailing various proposed works for Hinjewadi IT park.There are four roads proposed at Megapolis circle station with a length of 4.06 km. Roads proposed from this station will be developed by MIDC and gram panchayat. At Quadron circle station, three roads will be built stretching over 3.7 km and developed by MIDC. PMRDA will develop 1.5 km of road starting at Dohler circle station and another 1.1 km road from Wipro Technologies station. MIDC will construct a 500 m road at Infosys phase 2 station. The width of these carriageways will be 18 metres wide.A total of 1.6 km of road will be developed at Pall India station, of which MIDC will build two roads of 400 and 780 metres while PMRDA will develop one road of 400 metres.Shivaji Chowk station, which is expected to be one of the busiest points on the Hinjewadi line, has five last-mile connectivity roads, of which three will be developed by MIDC and two by PMRDA. articles.title: A river running late: Why Lucknow got flooded days after the rain stopped
articles.summary: Lucknow flooding lingered days after rain as Gomti runoff from heavy upstream rainfall took 8–10 days to arrive; floodplain encroachment worsened inundation.
articles.body: LUCKNOW: The state capital has witnessed flooding in several neighbourhoods over the past few days, but officials say the waterlogging is not solely the outcome of local rainfall. Instead, it is the downstream result of an eight- to 10-day movement of runoff generated nearly 250km upstream, where exceptionally heavy rain across Gomti catchment travelled gradually to the state capital.On Monday afternoon, Gomti was measured at 106.99 metres at Hanuman Setu, below the danger mark of 109.50 metres and far below the historic high flood level of 110.85 metres recorded in 1971.Despite that, low-lying colonies including Faizullahganj, Ghaila, Daud Nagar and nearby areas remained inundated, highlighting how delayed river response and floodplain encroachment can trigger urban flooding even when river levels and discharge are not at record highs.Gomti originates at Gomat Taal in Pilibhit and flows through Shahjahanpur, Lakhimpur Kheri, Hardoi and Sitapur before reaching Lucknow, then continues through Barabanki, Ayodhya, Sultanpur, Jaunpur and Ghazipur to join Ganga.Irrigation department officials said the river’s average downstream travel is about 30km a day, meaning runoff produced in the upper catchment typically takes eight to 10 days to reach Lucknow. This travel time explains why the river continued to rise in the city even after the heaviest rainfall had ended.Rainfall data from Sept 25 to 27 shows the scale of precipitation across districts feeding Gomti.Lakhimpur Kheri recorded 268.3mm against a normal of 7.3mm, while Shahjahanpur received 263.9mm against 5.3mm. Hardoi recorded 147.2mm against 4.1mm, Sitapur 144.1mm against 7.5mm, and Pilibhit 119.9mm against 8.6mm. Lucknow recorded 180.5mm during the same three-day spell compared with a normal of 9.4mm.Hydrologists said the cumulative rainfall across the upstream basin, rather than Lucknow’s rainfall alone, determines how much water ultimately reaches the city. Runoff generated across Pilibhit, Shahjahanpur, Lakhimpur Kheri, Hardoi and Sitapur continued feeding Gomti as it moved downstream, sustaining the river’s rise even as skies cleared over Lucknow.Before entering the city, Gomti also receives inflows from tributaries including Kathina, Sarayan, Gon, Behta and Kukrail, as well as multiple seasonal streams, adding to discharge during and after intense rain.The delayed flood pulse has been reflected in gauge readings at Hanuman Setu. The level rose from 106.55 metres on Oct 2 to 106.63 metres on Oct 3, 106.80 metres on Oct 4, 106.94 metres on Oct 5 morning, and touched 107 metres later the same day.Officials said the flooding has occurred even as discharge remains well below historical extremes. The irrigation department estimates about 40,000 cusecs are currently passing through Lucknow. The barrage was designed to handle 1.25 lakh cusecs.During the Sept 10, 1971, flood, when Gomti reached 110.85 metres, the barrage handled 1.07 lakh cusecs. In 1985, when the river touched the danger level of 109.50 metres, discharge was around 74,000 cusecs.Anil Garg, principal secretary of the irrigation and water resources department, attributed the inundation to three factors acting together: exceptionally heavy basin-wide rainfall, smaller rivers and streams reaching maximum carrying capacity after intense precipitation, and the urbanisation or encroachment of Gomti’s floodplain.Garg said the river historically spread over a wider floodplain during high flows, allowing floodwaters to disperse and recede gradually. With large sections now occupied by concrete development, the river has less space to spread evenly, forcing flows through a narrower corridor and increasing inundation in low-lying localities built on former floodplain areas.Officials expect gradual improvement if there is no fresh heavy rainfall in upstream districts. With the runoff generated during the Sept 25 to 27 spell nearing the end of its travel time to Lucknow, Gomti is expected to stabilise by Tuesday evening and begin a gradual recession from Wednesday morning.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: We're saving £100 a month into pensions for our toddler and baby - here's why
articles.summary: A growing number of parents are opening retirement funds for their children.
articles.body:
Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.

The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules.

So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.

Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing.

"Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."

'We don't eat out as often as we used to'

Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.

He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.

In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.

The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.

Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past.

"We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain.

"And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."

'I want to retire earlier so this will help'

Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.

The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show.

One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open as in the same period a year earlier.

Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.

While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?

Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years.

"The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."

Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.

For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity.

"Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."

It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.

In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.

Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.

Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.

"My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

"For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt.

"I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."

articles.title: Europe is pouring billions into space. Can Glasgow's satellite industry keep up?
articles.summary: The city's space boom raises questions about the role of the state in backing important industries.
articles.body:
In 2005, a young space engineer called Craig Clark moved back to his home city of Glasgow. He'd graduated from university just over a decade before, but the only jobs he could find were south of the border. Now Craig wanted to start a company of his own. He called it Clyde Space.

I went to school not far from the River Clyde, where the city's shipbuilding heritage was forged, and knew Glasgow had once been an industrial powerhouse. When I was a child, "Clyde-built" really meant something: craftsmanship and engineering excellence. There was a saying that I grew up with: "The Clyde made Glasgow and Glasgow made the Clyde."

What I hadn't realised until recently was that, in a different guise, that tradition is still alive. Two decades later, Glasgow is a European leader in building small satellites.

Many of those built here are known as CubeSats. Their basic building block measures just 10cm by 10cm by 10cm - think of something about the size of a Rubik's Cube. They are much smaller, cheaper and quicker to develop than the huge contraptions that you might picture when you think of satellites.

But crucially, they are modular and can be stacked together, then packed with cameras, sensors, communications equipment or other technology depending on their purpose.

And their size belies their significance. The data collected by satellites of all kinds is increasingly woven into everyday life. It helps us communicate and navigate, track ships and transport goods, monitor forests and crops, manage energy networks and understand changes to our climate.

For governments, that information can help inform decisions and respond to emergencies. As satellites have become more capable, space has become increasingly important.

More than two decades after the first satellite company was established there, the Scottish Government says more small satellites are built in Glasgow than anywhere else in Europe.

Across Scotland, the wider space industry generated £335m in income in 2022-23 - up 69% in five years. Excluding traditional satellite television broadcasting, it employed 2,811 people, an increase of 81% over the same period.

But elsewhere in Europe, governments are committing big money to their own satellite industries.

Could this take investment and jobs away from Glasgow? And if so, what - if anything - should the Scottish and UK governments do about it? And what should be the role of the state when it comes to backing important industries?

Glasgow's rise to small satellite superpower

Perhaps the most surprising thing about Glasgow's success in the space industry is that it wasn't planned.

One of the catalysts was Craig Clark's Clyde Space. The company specialised in CubeSats at just the right moment, a few years after it launched, as smaller and cheaper spacecraft were taking off, and would go on to build Scotland's first satellite, the UKube-1.

Crucially, the tech was built in partnership with the University of Strathclyde - which provided skills and research, as well as a ready supply of engineers.

Other companies followed, including Craft Prospect and Alba Orbital. Expertise grew and a new space cluster began to form. American satellite company Spire chose Glasgow for its European base in 2015. Smaller businesses developed, while established engineering and technology firms became part of the supply chain.

"Companies started moving to Glasgow because they could see that it was possible to do it here, and there was an ecosystem that was starting to grow," says Andrew Strain, chief technology officer at AAC Clyde Space - the company formed after Clyde Space was acquired by Swedish firm AAC Microtec, although Glasgow remains the group's main satellite manufacturing site.

Soon Glasgow was host to an "entire small satellite value chain", from components and satellite manufacturing, through to launch, spaceports and ground stations, according to Daniel Smith, founder of space marketing firm AstroAgency and the Scottish Government's trade and investment envoy for space.

There are wider benefits too. According to a review commissioned by Space Scotland, space manufacturing alone accounted for more than 1,000 Scottish jobs in 2022-23. The wider industry generated £202m for the Scottish economy.

And as the industry grew, so did the pool of knowledge. There are now more than 100 people working across space-related activity at the University of Strathclyde, with the subject now one of the institution's strategic priorities, according to Prof Malcolm Macdonald, its chair of applied space technology. The university works directly with commercial space companies on research and tech development.

Macdonald recalls that when he graduated, there was basically no local space industry for him to join. Now, "when our graduates leave the university, they will go and work in the local space sector because it is now here in Glasgow for them", he says.

But what's significant, Macdonald says, is that Glasgow's satellite industry wasn't something the government set out to establish. Instead, the process was "largely organic", says Smith.

By any measure it's a success story. But there are warnings about competition from overseas.

"It's not necessarily that we're going backwards," Macdonald tells me. "But other people are catching up."

Bavaria is emerging as a significant European hub for aerospace and defence technology. Germany's Defence Ministry says it plans to invest around €35bn (£30bn) in military space capabilities in the coming years, including more than 100 encrypted communications satellites.

For Macdonald, that kind of spending is changing Europe's space industry. Against a backdrop of the war in Ukraine and wider geopolitical uncertainty, governments are no longer simply supporting research and innovation. Increasingly, they are becoming major customers rather than just investors.

Will Lecky, co-founder and director of know.space, the space economics consultancy, says that matters because the global playing field is not level. He says UK public space funding falls well behind countries such as France and Germany.

"It's certainly a risk to Glasgow and the wider UK space sector that investment will follow the money and lead to longer term competitive disadvantage as activity flows elsewhere," he says.

Meanwhile, Finland's aerospace firm ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR), satellites, which can produce images of the Earth's surface through cloud and darkness. Macdonald says these have been used in the war in Ukraine, where satellite imagery can provide intelligence - for example, spotting a Russian vessel in a Crimean port - when conventional optical cameras cannot.

In June, ICEYE announced a funding round worth more than €1bn, valuing the company at more than €10bn. The Finnish state has also increased its stake and now owns around 12% of the company.

Finland's Minister for European Affairs, Joakim Strand, said the geopolitical situation had highlighted the importance of domestic ownership in what he called a "key strategic sector".

Governments want guaranteed access to satellite communications, especially when their country is facing a crisis. Some want the satellites - and the ability to build them - within their own borders.

"The recent increases in space spending elsewhere in Europe matter," says Gabriele Piazza, an economist at the London School of Economics who researches government procurement of advanced technology.

Space is not a normal market. Where the contracts go can help determine where companies invest, where engineers work and where expertise builds.

"Since capabilities build on themselves, firms with a large customer at home gain an advantage that lasts," Piazza adds.

Meanwhile, as well as Clyde Space's 2018 acquisition by AAC Microtec, Glasgow-founded Alba Orbital has moved its headquarters to the US, while retaining a Scottish base and team. Spire has expanded its manufacturing operation into Munich.

The Scottish government maintains that Glasgow still builds more small satellites than anywhere else in Europe. So, this is not an industry in decline.

But the bigger challenge, Smith says, is helping companies that start in Scotland to scale here.

"I wouldn't want it to be overly negative," says Macdonald. "It's more just like there are warning lights flashing that other parts of Europe are investing much more aggressively, and moving much more quickly, than we have."

Satellite camera manufacturer Simera Sense announced this year that it was opening a new production facility in the city, creating 20 highly skilled jobs. The firm, which has premises in South Africa, Belgium and France, will open a high-value electronics assembly lab and office at EastWorks in Dalmarnock.

That suggests something more nuanced than an exodus. Glasgow's concentration of universities, engineers and specialist suppliers, built up over two decades, would be difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Plus, some comparisons with overseas competitors are not exact. ICEYE is just one specialist company focused on radar satellites, while Glasgow is an entire manufacturing cluster producing different kinds of small satellites. Spire expanding in Munich does not necessarily mean it is retreating from Glasgow.

Smith doesn't think the answer is simply trying to outspend competitors: "We can grow alongside them," he says.

Instead, he argues Scotland should focus on what the industry actually needs – filling gaps and helping space companies find customers in areas such as energy, transport and healthcare.

With a successful domestic industry facing competition from abroad, you might anticipate calls for the government to provide financial support.

But Lecky cautions against that. He argues Glasgow's small satellite industry originally grew partly because of a lack of government support, as part of the commercially-focused "newspace" revolution.

"We shouldn't jump to government support as being the answer - it's critical to keep this commercial-minded attitude," he says.

"If you offered most entrepreneurs a choice between a grant, with significant paperwork, milestone payments and continuous scrutiny, or a paying customer, I suspect they would always choose the customer," he says.

And increasingly, governments are becoming that customer anyway.

For Smith, government contracts can do something grants cannot - give young companies revenue, a customer and a track record they can use to win business overseas.

Piazza says there is an economic case for thinking about procurement too. Building satellites creates knowledge that can spread far beyond the company itself. Engineers move between employers. Suppliers acquire new skills. Ideas become new products - sometimes in entirely different industries.

"Often, tomorrow's industries grow out of today's," he says. "The teams and suppliers building satellites now are the ones able to develop the next generation of a related technology, and once they disperse, they are very hard to reassemble."

Piazza points out that money spent supporting one industry cannot be spent on hospitals or schools. Governments can be poor at picking industries. And if everyone subsidises, nobody necessarily gains ground.

That is one reason procurement can make sense. The government buys something it needs anyway. The company gets a customer. Not just a grant.

But that raises a bigger question, made more important by the Ukraine war: what does the UK actually need to be able to do for itself?

Satellites provide communications, navigation and intelligence during conflict. Beyond defence, satellite services underpin parts of transport, energy, telecommunications and emergency response. Governments therefore have to decide which capabilities they are comfortable buying from overseas providers or allies.

Piazza says there can be a strategic case for keeping capabilities that are critical and difficult to replace. He describes it as a form of insurance. But keeping capability at home can mean higher costs, smaller production runs and duplicating what allies already do.

There is evidence that some public investment in space produces significant economic returns. Every £1 of UK investment through the European Space Agency generated £7.49 in direct economic benefit, an independent evaluation commissioned by the UK Space Agency estimated.

The UK Space Agency also says its work helped catalyse £2.2bn in investment and revenue for the UK space sector in 2024-25. But these figures relate to the whole of the UK, not Glasgow specifically.

The more important question may be where the valuable parts of the industry - its people, intellectual property, research and manufacturing - ultimately end up.

"The risk is not closure," says Piazza. "It is that the next phase of growth follows the contracts elsewhere."

Scotland also has another potential addition on the horizon: SaxaVord Spaceport in Shetland.

China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?

My hometown shows that high streets have to change or die

The vision of a fully integrated, "end-to-end" space sector is moving closer to reality. Although the infrastructure is ready, actual launch campaigns have experienced technical delays.

"We are in a great position right now," says Strain. "But if we get complacent, then we can fall behind again because it's moving very, very fast."

Glasgow's shipyards once made the city synonymous with building things for the world. Its space industry has done something similar - almost by accident.

The question now is not whether Glasgow can build a successful satellite industry. It already has.

It is whether the next phase of that success is built here too.

articles.title: MPs call for investigation after Howard  Lutnick-Jeffrey Epstein whistleblower dies
articles.summary: Simon Andriesz said he felt let down by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority before his death last month.
articles.body:
The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said.

Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand.

Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender.

A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation.

Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play.

How US commerce secretary's Epstein links were uncovered by British whistleblower

Andriesz uncovered evidence that Lutnick had sought, in Andriesz's words, to "buy a prince", offering to go into business with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2013 and utilise the former prince's contacts to attract investments, in exchange for a loan of £1m. BGC told the BBC the proposed joint venture did not go ahead.

Andriesz also submitted evidence to the FCA to support his allegations of misconduct at Lutnick's former firm, including an allegation that cash from the pool of commission money set aside to pay brokers' bonuses was "embezzled" for improper purposes – an allegation the firm has denied.

Weeks before his death, Andriesz told a public event led by MPs, whistleblowers and campaigners calling for fairer regulation that he felt "thoroughly let down" and had been put through "absolute hell" by the FCA, to whom he had sent evidence of what he regarded as whistleblower retaliation by BGC and its lawyers.

The FCA had previously told Andriesz there was "insufficient evidence" to conclude there had been retaliation, a conclusion he believed made it harder to win a claim against BGC at tribunal.

BGC previously told the BBC it had strong policies protecting whistleblowers and denied retaliating against him.

John McDonnell, the Labour backbench MP and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services, described Andriesz's death as a "profound and preventable tragedy".

He said whistleblowers were "an essential part of the financial regulatory system" and warned there would be consequences for the integrity of the system if people did not believe they would be "treated properly, protected appropriately and listened to seriously".

The group of MPs called for the FCA to pay for an independent party to evaluate its handling of whistleblowers.

In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction.

The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information.

But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal.

Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations.

"It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said.

The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations.

An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends.

"Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future."

articles.title: Lula venceu em 64 países; Flávio Bolsonaro, em 36: veja MAPA | G1
articles.standfirst: Em apenas um país, os dois candidatos empataram no 1º turno. Em 32 dos 133 territórios com votação, nenhum eleitor compareceu às urnas.
articles.summary: Em apenas um país, os dois candidatos empataram no 1º turno. Em 32 dos 133 territórios com votação, nenhum eleitor compareceu às urnas.
articles.body:
Mapa mostra como foram as eleições no exterior — Foto: Kayan Albertin/Arte g1

Lula (PT) terminou o primeiro turno da eleição presidencial na liderança entre os brasileiros que vivem no exterior. Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) ficou em segundo lugar. Ao todo, o petista venceu em 64 países, enquanto o senador liderou em 36. Houve empate em um território.

Os dados foram consolidados pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) no domingo (4). Ao todo, 916.534 brasileiros estão aptos a votar no exterior. No 1º turno, foram instaladas urnas em 186 cidades de 133 países e territórios, incluindo a Guiana Francesa.

Segundo o TSE, apesar do grande número de brasileiros aptos a votar no exterior, 62,69% não compareceram às urnas. Entre os que votaram, 10.884 eleitores optaram pelo voto em branco ou nulo.

Lula teve 47,57% dos votos válidos no exterior, o equivalente a 157.387.

Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 143.900, ou 43,49%.

Na sequência aparecem Escritor Augusto Cury (2,94%), Renan Santos (2,59%), Ronaldo Caiado (1,42%) e Romeu Zema (1,01%).

Os demais candidatos não alcançaram 1% dos votos válidos.

▶️ Confira a seguir como foi a votação por região.

Confira como foi a disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro na América — Foto: Kayan Albertin/Arte g1

Mais de um terço dos votos no exterior se concentrou no continente americano. Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 63.737 votos na região, contra 44.793 de Lula. O desempenho do senador foi puxado principalmente pelo resultado nos EUA, onde ele teve quase o dobro de votos do petista.

Os Estados Unidos foram o país onde Flávio recebeu mais votos: 45.004.

O senador também venceu em outros 18 países da região, como Bolívia, Colômbia, El Salvador e Equador.

O melhor desempenho de Flávio em votos válidos no exterior foi registrado em Salto del Guairá, no Paraguai, onde o índice chegou a 94,48%.

Lula liderou em oito países, entre eles Argentina, Canadá, Chile, Uruguai e Venezuela. No Haiti, foi o único candidato a receber votos. Apenas cinco eleitores, no entanto, votaram no país.

Em quatro países onde havia urnas, nenhum eleitor compareceu: Antígua e Barbuda, Barbados, Belize e Santa Lúcia.

⚠️ Os dados da América não incluem os votos registrados no Brasil.

Veja como foi a disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro na Europa — Foto: Kayan Albertin/Arte g1

Lula foi o candidato mais votado na Europa e venceu em 25 dos 29 países com urnas na região. O petista recebeu 95.442 votos, contra 48.874 de Flávio. Países como Reino Unido, Alemanha, França e Espanha puxaram o desempenho de Lula no continente.

Em Portugal, segundo país com mais eleitores brasileiros aptos a votar no exterior, Lula foi escolhido por 26.401 eleitores, contra 19.412 de Flávio. Também foi o país onde o petista recebeu mais votos no exterior.

Ainda em Portugal, Lula venceu em Lisboa e no Porto. Flávio, por outro lado, liderou em Faro, na região do Algarve.

Lula perdeu em apenas dois países europeus: Grécia e Ucrânia, ambos com poucos eleitores. Em Kiev, por exemplo, Flávio teve 19 votos, enquanto Lula recebeu 4.

Nenhum eleitor compareceu às urnas na Albânia e na Bósnia-Herzegovina.

Disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro no 1º turno, na Ásia — Foto: Kayan Albertin/Arte g1

Flávio Bolsonaro foi o mais votado na Ásia , apesar de ter vencido em menos países. O senador recebeu 28.063 votos e liderou em 13 países. Lula teve 11.643 votos e venceu em 15.

O resultado favorável a Flávio foi puxado principalmente pelo Japão, terceiro país com mais eleitores brasileiros aptos a votar no exterior. Lá, o senador teve quase cinco vezes mais votos que Lula.

Além do Japão, Flávio venceu em países como Catar, Emirados Árabes Unidos, Israel e Vietnã.

Lula liderou em territórios como Arábia Saudita, China, Líbano e Palestina.

Mumbai, na Índia, foi a única cidade no exterior onde Flávio ficou em terceiro lugar. Ele teve apenas 1 voto, contra 3 de Renan Santos e 5 de Lula.

Em 10 países com urnas, nenhum eleitor compareceu. Entre eles estão Armênia, Azerbaijão, Cazaquistão, Iraque e Paquistão.

Na Oceania , Lula foi o mais votado e venceu nos dois países com urnas: Austrália e Nova Zelândia.

Na Austrália , Lula teve 4.562 votos, contra 2.579 de Flávio.

Na Nova Zelândia , Lula recebeu 234 votos, enquanto Flávio teve 64.

Disputa entre Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro na África, no 1º turno — Foto: Kayan Albertin/Arte g1

Apesar de haver urnas em 33 países africanos, a região foi onde menos eleitores brasileiros votaram. Lula recebeu 713 votos e liderou em 14 países. Flávio teve 583 votos e ficou à frente em dois.

Lula venceu em países como Angola, Marrocos, Nigéria e Senegal.

Na Líbia, o petista teve 100% dos votos, mas apenas dois eleitores compareceram às urnas.

Flávio liderou na África do Sul e em Moçambique.

Em 16 países com urnas, nenhum eleitor compareceu. Entre eles estão Camarões, Etiópia e Zimbábue.

Foi também na África que ocorreu o único empate do 1º turno no exterior. Na Guiné-Bissau, Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro receberam 17 votos cada.

articles.title: A única cidade no exterior em que Flávio Bolsonaro não ficou entre os dois primeiros | G1
articles.standfirst: Eleição no exterior repetiu a polarização da disputa presidencial de 2022, mas teve resultado diferente em um dos países onde houve votação.
articles.summary: Eleição no exterior repetiu a polarização da disputa presidencial de 2022, mas teve resultado diferente em um dos países onde houve votação.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro fala após ida ao 2º turno — Foto: EVARISTO SA/AFP

Neste domingo (4), brasileiros foram às urnas em diferentes partes do mundo para escolher quem ocupará a Presidência da República pelos próximos quatro anos. A disputa foi marcada — mais uma vez — pela polarização entre Lula (PT) e um candidato do Partido Liberal (PL), desta vez Flávio Bolsonaro .

No entanto, apesar da disputa acirrada entre os dois candidatos, que resultou em um 2º turno, houve uma única cidade no exterior em que um candidato diferente figurou entre a primeiras colocações: Mumbai, na Índia.

Por lá, Lula ficou em primeiro com 5 votos, porém a segunda a colocação ficou com Renan Santos (Missão), com 3 votos. Flávio Bolsonaro, por sua vez, recebeu apenas um voto.

Ao todo, 57 pessoas estavam aptas a votar para presidente na metrópole indiana, porém apenas 11 eleitores compareceram às urnas.

Somando todas as seções eleitorais da Índia, Lula teve 29 votos (47,54%), contra 27 votos (44,26%) de Flávio e 3 votos (4,92%) de Renan Santos.

Lula ou Flávio Bolsonaro não aparecerem entre os dois primeiros colocados é algo raro. A única cidade em que a situaçã se repetiu foi em Guarani de Goiás, onde Ronaldo Caiado ficou em segundo lugar, com 32,26% dos votos, enquanto Flávio terminou na terceira colocação, com 26,64%.

Renan Santos, do Missão, candidato à Presidência — Foto: Globo/ Manoella Mello

Os votos deste primeiro turno mostram um resultado difrente em alguns países quando comparado às eleições de 2022, quando Lula enfrentou o pai de Flávio, Jair Bolsonaro.

No Kuwait, por exemplo, onde Bolsonaro foi o mais votado há quatro anos, o petista venceu desta vez. Na Tailândia, o movimento foi inverso: o país que deu a maior votação ao atual presidente em 2022 teve Flávio como o mais votado em 2026.

Lula também voltou a vencer em países como Portugal, França, Alemanha e Reino Unido. Flávio, por sua vez, foi o mais votado no Japão e em Israel, onde seu pai havia vencido na eleição anterior.

Portugal : Lula voltou a vencer, com 52,45%. No primeiro turno de 2022, o petista recebeu 60,4%.

Israel : Flávio foi o mais votado, com 74,40%. Jair Bolsonaro venceu no país em 2022, com 46%.

Estados Unidos : Flávio foi o mais votado com 61,1% dos votos. Em 2022, Jair Bolsonaro venceu por 57,9%.

Alemanha : Lula venceu com 74,58%. Em 2022 o petista também saiu vitorioso, com 69,4%.

França : Lula venceu por 78,39%. Em 2022, o atual preseidente também venceu por 77,6%.

Candidatos mais votados por país no primeiro turno de 2022 e de 2026, segundo dados do TSE. Síria participa pela primeira vez. — Foto: Arte/g1

No primeiro turno das eleições de 2022, cerca de 696 mil brasileiros estavam inscritos para votar fora do país. Esse grupo representava aproximadamente 0,45% do eleitorado brasileiro, que era de 156,5 milhões de pessoas.

A participação foi de 44,76% dos eleitores inscritos no exterior. Entre os que compareceram, 1,60% votaram em branco e 1,53% anularam o voto.

Lula recebeu 47,17% dos votos válidos no exterior e foi o mais votado em 85 cidades. Entre os países onde venceu estavam Portugal, Palestina, Reino Unido e França.

Jair Bolsonaro recebeu 41,61% dos votos válidos no exterior e foi o mais votado em 54 cidades. Ele venceu em países como Estados Unidos, Japão, Israel e Paraguai.

articles.summary: A equipe de Lula cogita trocas no comando da estratégia e fala em 'ir pra cima' de Flávio. Já o presidente do PL fala sobre um possível governo com a participação de Jair Bolsonaro.
articles.body:
No dia seguinte às urnas, as campanhas dos dois candidatos presidenciáveis têm tons diferentes. A equipe de Lula cogita trocas no comando da estratégia e fala em pautar o debate de propostas e em "ir pra cima" de Flávio. Do lado do candidato da oposição, Valdemar da Costa Neto, presidente do PL, partido que abriga a família Bolsonaro, já fala sobre um possível governo e cita até a participação do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro num eventual mandato de Flávio.

articles.title: Newspaper headlines: Badenoch's 'Britannia Dome' and 'King tells Andrew 'I won't fund court fight''
articles.summary: Several of Tuesday's papers lead on a Tory pledge to devote £10bn to an Iron Dome-style defence system.
articles.body:
Pictures of Jeffrey Archer are on many of the front pages, following his death at the age of 86. The Times says he was "well aware that the sands of time" were running out on his life, which was "even stranger than fiction". Broadcaster Gyles Brandreth is quoted in the Daily Telegraph saying that he'd been with the novelist on Sunday, and he'd been "funny, engaging and self-deprecating". The Daily Star's front page notes that Jeffrey Archer had sued the paper, and then been jailed for perjury. The Daily Mail concluded that he'd had a "colourful life", but was a "great storyteller" until the end.

"Britain needs an iron dome" is the headline in the Daily Express , which leads with the Conservatives' pledge to spend £10bn on a missile defence system. The i questions how realistic that price tag is - given that previous estimates for the project have been at least £80bn. The Sun notes that this announcement came just as the US was pulling its bombers out of RAF Fairford because of safety concerns.

The Daily Mirror headlines on the King's warning to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor: "don't use my money" to pay for a legal fight with police. The Daily Telegraph says this appears to be the monarch's latest effort to "distance" himself from his brother's decision to sue the Thames Valley Police force.

The front page of the Guardian highlights a study showing that seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England. The paper says a team of scientists from the World Cancer Research Fund believe that's a sign of rising levels of obesity, poor diets and insufficient exercise, as well as better awareness and earlier diagnosis.

Have you had a coffee yet today? The Express picks up on a study which shows that a typical coffee drinker consumes almost 57,000 cups worth in their lifetime - an average of 2-and-a-half a day. And most people have their first between 07:00 and 08:00.

The i writes that the project "would link new radar, command systems and interceptor missiles" into a single network. The pledge is an attempt by party leader Kemi Badenoch to "build credibility" on defence, the paper says, but critics say the £10bn price tag is well below previous cost estimates of at least £80bn

articles.title: Australian soldier killed and five injured in crash during training exercise
articles.summary: A vehicle rolled over on Monday at the Mount Bundey training area, southeast of Darwin.
articles.body:
An Australian soldier has died and five others have been injured in a crash during a training exercise in the Northern Territory (NT).

Police said a vehicle had rolled over at the Mount Bundey training area, about 130km (80 mi) southeast of Darwin, on Monday afternoon.

One man was declared dead at the scene while five others were airlifted to hospital in Darwin.

The area - used by the army for live fire training - is the same location where Jason Challis was killed in 2017 after he was shot in the head during an exercise. The department later pleaded guilty for failing to comply with workplace safety.

Monday's incident caused the second death of an Australian soldier this year after a paratrooper died after a mid-air collision during training in May.

The Department of Defence confirmed the incident on Tuesday but gave no further details and requested the privacy of the soldiers and families affected be respected.

NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said two injured soldiers had been taken to the Royal Darwin Hospital by helicopter and another three by plane on Monday evening, according to national broadcaster ABC.

"Our thoughts and prayers are with the family who are obviously devastated by this loss and of course, the support of our entire community is there for all of our service personnel who will be feeling this loss immensely," she said.

The ABC also reported that the NT Police Commissioner Martin Dole had sent resources to the Mount Bundey training area to help with the department's investigation into the incident.

"We can't comment on the cause of the injury to the defence personnel but we are assisting and were helping to investigate on behalf of the coroner," Dole said, according to the ABC.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his thoughts were with the family and friends of the victims, adding: "There are no safe or easy days for those who serve in our country's name."

During a 2019 inquest into the death of Challis, a 25-year-old soldier from Victoria, the coroner described the training exercise as "shambolic" and that his death had been preventable.

Challis, who had less than a year's experience with the defence force, was shot in the head and knee while he stood behind a plywood wall during an urban attack exercise.

In May this year, Lachlan Muddle - a Special Air Service Regiment soldier - died when he fell to the ground after a mid-air collision with another paratrooper at the Jervis Bay airfield in New South Wales.

articles.title: Waymo recalls 672 driverless vehicles after Phoenix taxi hits utility pole, prompting software and map updates to help cars avoid fixed objects
articles.summary: Waymo, self-driving arm of Alphabet, said on Thursday, 13 June 2024, that it would recall 672 driverless vehicles.
articles.body: Waymo, self-driving arm of Alphabet, said on Thursday, 13 June 2024, that it would recall 672 driverless vehicles. The recall followed a collision in May in which one vehicle struck a wooden utility pole in an alleyway in Phoenix, Arizona, while attempting a low-speed pullover manoeuvre. According to Reuters, no passengers, other road users or injuries were involved. Waymo has installed a software update and mapping improvements across the fleet. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has also been examining 22 reports of Waymo robotaxis behaving unexpectedly, including 17 collisions.How did Waymo’s mapping updates help its driverless cars avoid polesAccording to the Associated Press, Waymo has completed a software update that improves how the automated driving system responds to poles and pole-like permanent objects. Reuters says the same remedy was part of the recall, and NHTSA stated that, before the update, the system could fail to avoid a pole or similar object. Waymo is saying "robust mapping updates and improvements" have already been installed in all of the vehicles. The map update adds a "hard road edge" between the pole or pole-like object and the drivable surface.NHTSA opened an investigation in May after receiving 22 reports of Waymo robotaxis behaving in ways that potentially violated traffic safety laws, or showing other unexpected behaviour. Seventeen of those reports involved collisions. Reuters adds that on the Wednesday before the recall announcement, NHTSA said it was seeking details about a series of incidents that had raised concerns about the performance of Waymo's driverless vehicles.What did NHTSA ask Waymo about its driverless vehicle incidentsThe regulator said several incidents involved collisions with clearly visible objects that a competent driver would be expected to avoid. Collisions with stationary and semi-stationary objects such as gates and chains, collisions with parked vehicles, and cases in which the driving system appeared to disobey traffic safety controls. NHTSA required Waymo to answer detailed questions by 6 August, including whether any vehicles had been grounded and whether tests or updates had been carried out to address specific incidents.Waymo had issued an earlier recall in February, covering 444 self-driving vehicles after two minor collisions in quick succession in Arizona. Waymo said at the time that a software error could cause its automated vehicles to inaccurately predict the presence of a towed vehicle. The latest recall is the most recent in a series of NHTSA investigations into the performance of self-driving vehicles, after the regulator opened probes into General Motors' Cruise and Amazon's Zoox. Waymo earlier said it was proud of its performance and safety record over tens of millions of autonomous miles driven.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Malik Hasan to die by US Army firing squad
articles.summary: Hasan, a former Army officer who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009, will be executed by firing squad.
articles.body:
Former Army officer Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and injured 32 others in a mass shooting at Fort Hood in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad as approved by President Donald J. Trump.

Hasan's execution by firing squad would be the first such case for the U.S. military since Pvt. Eddie D. Slovik was executed in 1945 for desertion during World War II.

Hasan admitted to the shooting during his court-martial in 2013, stating he carried out the attack in support of the Taliban, and was subsequently sentenced to death by a military jury.

Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army officer and psychiatrist who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday.

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell announced . "He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack.

"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution," he continued. "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come."

If Hasan's execution is indeed carried out by a firing squad, it would mark the first such case for the service since Jan. 31, 1945, when Pvt. Eddie D. Slovik was executed by a U.S. Army firing squad in France for desertion during World War II.

The last death sentence carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging at the gallows in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill a young girl.

Hasan, who was born in northern Virginia, walked into a Fort Hood readiness processing center on Nov. 5, 2009, and opened fire using a semi-automatic handgun.

Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier.

Former Army Staff Sgt. Patrick Zeigler, a two-time combat veteran, was shot four times in the attack and spent nearly a year recovering in various hospitals.

"He looked me straight in the eyes as he pointed the gun at me, and a split second later, I'm on the floor with a hole in my head," he told the Killeen Daily Herald in 2023.

At his court-martial, Hasan, now 56, admitted to the shooting, and in 2013 said he carried out the attack in support of the Taliban.

At the time, Hasan requested a delay in court proceedings so he could ready a new legal strategy that would show he acted "in defense of others."

Asked by presiding Judge Col. Tara Osborn who he was defending, Hasan replied , "The leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban."

Hasan was convicted by a military jury in August 2013, which recommended he be sentenced to death.

He was subsequently transferred to Fort Leavenworth, where he has been incarcerated on death row.

Jonathan Lehrfeld contributed to this report.

articles.title: Jeffrey Archer, British author and former conservative politician, dies at 86
articles.summary: Acclaimed author and former British politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86.
articles.body: Acclaimed author and former British politician Jeffrey Archer has died at the age of 86.HarperCollins, Archer’s publisher, said he died “suddenly and peacefully at home” on Monday, between writing sessions. Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK CEO and Archer’s editor, said: “We’re all devastated to have lost a writer who has brought joy to generations of readers — and a true friend.”Archer was a bestselling author who sold more than 300 million books during a five-decade writing career, was best known for novels including Kane and Abel and the Clifton Chronicles.Archer was also a former Conservative MP whose political career was derailed after he was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice. He was jailed in 2001 after being found guilty of lying during a libel case he had brought against the Daily Star.From Parliament to bestselling fictionArcher was born in North London on April 15, 1940.In 1969, he became one of the youngest members of the House of Commons after he was elected as the Conservative MP for Louth in Lincolnshire. He served in Parliament for five years before becoming deputy chairman of the Conservative Party.His political career came to an abrupt halt after the libel case against the Daily Star. Archer had initially won £500,000 in damages, but was later found to have lied about the circumstances surrounding the case.He was released from prison in 2003 and later returned to the House of Lords, where he remained until retiring in 2024.Tributes pour inArcher’s final novel, Adam and Eve, is due to be released this week. HarperCollins described him as a “master storyteller” and said his readers “meant everything to him”.Archer and his wife Mary celebrated their 60th wedding anniversary this year. They have two sons and five grandchildren.Conservative party leader Kemi Badenoch described his death as a “huge shock”, saying Archer had sent her a message on the morning of his death and had been “a great source of encouragement”.Former Conservative chancellor Nadhim Zahawi, who described Archer as a “dear friend”, also paid tribute to his wit, warmth and energy.“Life was never dull in Jeffrey's company,” Zahawi said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Donald Trump says ‘some threats’ prompted US to pull bombers from UK base
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump said Monday that \"some threats\" prompted the United States to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain, suggesting the
articles.body: US President Donald Trump said Monday that "some threats" prompted the United States to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford in Britain, suggesting the move was linked to a security concern at the airbase.Trump said the aircraft did not leave the base by chance and that Washington knew who had made the threat, although he did not identify the individuals or provide details about the nature of the threat.Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked whether a "specific threat" had led to the withdrawal of the bombers.Trump replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident."He added: "There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."The Pentagon confirmed Sunday that US bombers, believed to include around a dozen B-1 aircraft, had been moved from RAF Fairford back to their home stations in the United States.Bombers moved after airbase security alertTrump's remarks appear to reinforce reports that a new security threat prompted the redeployment following an incident near the airbase on September 27.British police had been alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" travelling towards RAF Fairford. Five men were subsequently arrested on suspicion of terrorism-related offences and later released on bail. A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested separately and also released on bail.Police have said no explosives were found in the vans involved in the initial security alert.Trump said Washington "actually knows the people that made the threat", but stopped short of identifying them.The exact nature of the threat remains unclear. US sources cited by British media have speculated that it could have involved possible sabotage or an attempt to target the expensive aircraft stationed at the base.One source close to the White House pointed to Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb, in which drones attacked Russian military bases, as an example of how an adversary could potentially strike sensitive military assets from a distance."Whatever they thought it was, it was taken extremely seriously," the source said.RAF Fairford, located in Gloucestershire's Cotswolds, hosts the headquarters of the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing and serves as a forward operating location for US Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has been used in previous US military operations, including the 1990 Gulf War and the 2003 Iraq war, as well as this year's US-Israeli bombardment of Iran.Washington divided over Iran linkThe developments have fuelled questions over whether the security incident was connected to Iran. British authorities have indicated that Iran may have been involved, while Tehran has denied any role.British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there are "strong indications" that Iran played a part in the incident, without providing details about what the suspects allegedly planned or the basis for the assessment.Laurence Taylor, head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, said investigators were examining whether the alleged offences were carried out by "proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."Iran's embassy in Britain rejected the allegations, condemning what it described as "unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets" linking Tehran to the suspected plot.Trump had earlier criticised the decision to release the first five suspects on bail and suggested Iran could have been involved.However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio adopted a more cautious position, refusing to directly link the police investigation to the withdrawal of the bombers.Rubio said: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."He said the US continued to have full confidence in the security of its bases and praised British authorities for their cooperation following the incident.US Vice President JD Vance said the bombers had been moved out of an "abundance of caution" and accused Iran of continuing a long-standing pattern of terrorism."We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they're trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engage in acts of terrorism against the United States and against a lot of other people as well. So, we are being extremely cautious," he said.British officials have meanwhile maintained that RAF Fairford is safe, leaving unanswered questions over what prompted Washington to move the bombers and whether the suspected plot was directly connected to Iran.You use AI every day.
