articles.title: A French geologist spent 205 days underground with no clock or daylight, and his body eventually treated almost 48 hours as a single day
articles.summary: Michel Siffre’s first descent was meant to be a geological expedition.
articles.body: Michel Siffre’s first descent was meant to be a geological expedition. Instead, it became an experiment in what happens when a person loses every ordinary clue to the passing of time. In 1962, the 23-year-old French speleologist entered a cave in the Alps and stayed there alone for 63 days, with no clock, calendar or sunlight. He ate, slept and worked according to signals from his own body while a team outside recorded what happened. By the time he emerged, Siffre believed far less time had passed than actually had. In an email interview by Joshua Foer, published in Cabinet's Summer 2008 issue, a decade later, he repeated the experiment in Texas, remaining underground for 205 days and occasionally falling into a sleep-wake cycle that stretched across almost 48 hours.French geologist Michel Siffre turned a cave expedition into a body clock experimentSiffre did not originally set out to investigate human timekeeping. He was trained as a geologist and had become interested in an underground glacier discovered in the Alps in 1961, roughly 70 kilometres from Nice. His initial plan was modest: spend around 15 days underground studying it.That seemed too short once he considered what he might actually observe. He decided to extend the stay to two months and, somewhere in the process, changed the experiment completely. Rather than simply studying the cave, he would remove himself from the ordinary markers of time and see what his body did without them.There would be no watch and no daylight. A small team would remain near the entrance, but it would not tell him the time or contact him unnecessarily. Siffre would call them when he woke, when he ate and before going to sleep. The researchers could then compare his reported routine with the actual passage of time outside.It was an unusually simple arrangement, but it separated his biological rhythms from the 24-hour cycle imposed by the surface environment.Inside the cave: Siffre’s sense of time began to unravelThe conditions were not comfortable. Siffre described his equipment as poor, with his small living area crowded with supplies. The cave was extremely damp and cold, with temperatures below freezing and humidity approaching 98 per cent. His feet remained wet and his body temperature at one point fell to about 34°C.There was little to do beyond reading, writing, carrying out research and thinking. A light bulb provided illumination, but there was no distinction between morning and evening, and no sunrise to announce the beginning of another day. Siffre's contact with the outside world was deliberately limited. Each time he called the surface, he measured his pulse and performed a simple psychological test. He was instructed to count from one to 120 at a rate of one number per second.The results revealed how far his internal sense of duration could drift. What should have taken two minutes according to the test took him around five minutes in his subjective experience. The passage of time inside the cave was no longer matching the clock outside.Siffre had entered the cave on 16 July and expected to remain there until 14 September. When his team finally told him that the agreed end date had arrived, he believed it was only around 20 August. He had effectively lost track of almost an entire month.Without daylight, the body kept its own scheduleThe experiment suggested that people do not simply stop having a rhythm when external clocks disappear. Instead, the body's own timing system continues to operate, although it does not necessarily follow exactly 24 hours. Siffre's sleep-wake cycle during the first experiment was roughly 24 and a half hours. He would decide for himself when to sleep and when to eat, without knowing what time it was on the surface.Later experiments with other people produced something even stranger. Some subjects developed cycles lasting close to 48 hours. Rather than sleeping every night, they could remain awake for roughly 36 hours and then sleep for 12 to 14 hours.The pattern was important because it showed how dramatically human behaviour could become separated from the familiar day-night cycle. The subjects were not being told to remain awake for longer. Their routines were emerging in an environment where the normal cues had been removed.Siffre himself did not consistently fall into the longer rhythm during his first experiment. That became one of the reasons he eventually decided to return underground.The cave became a laboratory for sleepSiffre's later experiments went beyond simply recording when people slept. His teams monitored different stages of sleep, including rapid eye movement, or REM, and slow-wave sleep. They reported a relationship between extended periods of wakefulness and the amount of REM sleep that followed. According to Siffre, approximately 10 additional minutes of activity was associated with about one extra minute of REM sleep.There was also an apparent connection with performance afterwards. Subjects who spent more time dreaming appeared to have shorter reaction times during their following waking period. The findings attracted interest from the French military, which was investigating whether soldiers might be able to remain operational for unusually long periods. Siffre's work was taking place during a period when sleep and biological rhythms had obvious military and spaceflight implications.France was developing its nuclear submarine programme, while the United States and Soviet Union were competing to send humans into space. Knowing how people might sleep when the usual 24-hour environment was absent had practical value.NASA also examined the results from Siffre's 1962 experiment and helped fund mathematical analysis of the data.He returned to the darkness in TexasTen years after his first experiment, Siffre went underground again. This time the setting was Midnight Cave near Del Rio, Texas. The second experiment lasted 205 days. There was a personal scientific question behind it. Siffre wanted to examine how his perception of time might change as he aged, and he also wanted to see whether he could eventually develop the 48-hour rhythm that had appeared in several of his other subjects.The Texas experiment was considerably more elaborate than the first. Electrodes were used to monitor physiological activity, including signals associated with the heart, brain and muscles. Yet the basic principle remained: Siffre was separated from the outside world's clocks and natural light. He was left to determine his own periods of sleep, eating and activity.At times, the experiment produced the long cycle he had been looking for. On two occasions, he experienced periods of about 36 hours of wakefulness followed by roughly 12 hours of sleep.A 48-hour day did not feel like a 48-hour dayPerhaps the most revealing part of the Texas experiment was that Siffre could not reliably tell which sort of day he was experiencing. A period of wakefulness lasting 36 hours did not necessarily feel unusually long to him. A much shorter period could feel similar. His diary allowed him to reconstruct the cycles afterwards, but his own perception provided little warning that one of his biological days had stretched to almost twice the conventional length.He also described sleeping for dramatically different amounts of time, sometimes only two hours and sometimes as long as 18 hours, without having a clear subjective sense of how different those episodes were. The distinction between measured time and experienced time had become central to his work.For someone living underground, the disappearance of daylight removed one of the most powerful signals used to organise everyday life. There was no sunrise after sleep, no changing sky during waking hours and no evening darkness arriving at a predictable point. The cave remained essentially the same. Siffre later suggested that memory itself might contribute to the effect. With little changing around a person, individual days become difficult to distinguish from one another. Waking and sleeping provide the main divisions, while everything in between takes place against the same darkness.The experiments had consequences beyond cavesSiffre's work became part of the emerging study of human biological rhythms, now known as chronobiology. The central observation was straightforward: humans possess internal timing mechanisms, and those mechanisms can continue operating even when the external cues normally used to regulate them are removed.The research also intersected with questions that were becoming increasingly important in spaceflight and military operations. Astronauts and submariners could spend long periods away from ordinary patterns of daylight and night. Crews working irregular shifts faced related problems.The military interest in Siffre's findings was particularly strong during the Cold War. Researchers wanted to understand whether human wakefulness could be extended without simply exhausting the person involved. Some of the ideas were experimental and never became practical methods. The French army, for example, explored whether medication could increase REM sleep in the hope of manipulating the length of an individual's waking period.The cave experiments nevertheless provided something difficult to obtain in a conventional laboratory: people were living for weeks or months without knowing what time it was.One subject slept for 33 hoursThe risks were considerable, especially by modern research standards. During one early experiment in 1964, a man being monitored underground slept for 33 hours. Because he had a microphone attached to his head, the researchers could listen for signs that he was still alive. For a long period, they heard nothing.Siffre eventually decided he needed to enter the cave to check on him. At about the 34-hour mark, the sleeper snored. A short time later, he contacted the surface himself and asked the team to take his pulse.The episode illustrates how differently these experiments were conducted in the 1960s compared with modern human research. Siffre later acknowledged that current ethical oversight would make such an approach far more difficult. A subject who remained asleep for that long would be regarded as a medical concern rather than simply another unexpected result.The willingness to accept that level of uncertainty was partly a product of the period in which the experiments took place.His final cave experiments came decades laterSiffre's long spell in Texas also had a financial cost. He had underestimated the expense of transporting the equipment and running the operation in the United States, and he emerged from the cave with substantial debts. He eventually moved away from chronobiology.It was not until 1999 that he returned underground, this time to Clamouse Cave in southern France. He was interested in the effects of ageing on the circadian cycle and wanted to compare his experience with his earlier experiments.The timing was deliberate. Siffre had been inspired in part by astronaut John Glenn, who returned to space at the age of 77. Siffre saw a similar opportunity to revisit a question he had first explored as a young man and examine whether his perception of time had changed with age. He spent two months underground.By then, the era of the great isolation experiments was largely coming to an end. Modern research ethics placed much greater limits on the degree of risk researchers could ask human subjects to accept, making prolonged isolation in a cave much harder to justify.You use AI every day. articles.body: BHOPAL: Project Cheetah crossed another milestone on Sunday with the birth of five cubs at MP's Kuno National Park, taking India's total cheetah count to 60, including 41 born in the country.The cubs were born to 32-month-old cheetah KJ, making her the third India-born female to give birth in the country after Mukhi and KGP12, Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav announced in a social media post, describing it as "an important milestone in the emergence of the next generation of India's cheetah population".The development is an important marker in the progress of Project Cheetah, which aims not only to establish a viable population of the feline in India 70 years after it was declared extinct, but also to enable the species to breed and sustain itself over successive generations, say officials.The birth has an added genetic significance. The father of the five cubs is a male brought from Botswana, making them the first India-born cheetahs to carry the Botswanan lineage. articles.title: 'Army to set time & place': Trump approves firing squad execution for 2009 Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, who killed 13
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: US President Donald Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Army Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who was convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood massacre in Texas that killed 13 people and wounded 32 others.The Pentagon announced Monday night that defense secretary Pete Hegseth had recommended a firing squad for Hasan's execution and Trump had approved the recommendation.Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on X that Hegseth would determine the time and place of the execution.“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell wrote.Parnell described Hasan as “the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009.” He said Hasan “killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting ‘Allahu Akbar’ during the attack.”Hasan convicted in 2009 Fort Hood attackHasan, an Army psychiatrist, entered a medical building at Fort Hood where soldiers were undergoing medical examinations and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.He shouted “Allahu akbar”, Arabic for “God is great”, during the attack.Hasan said the shooting was intended to stop US soldiers from deploying to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He made little effort to defend himself during his trial and told jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter.He described himself as a soldier who had “switched sides.”Trump's approval sets in motion a series of procedural steps towards carrying out the execution. However, Hasan could seek a habeas corpus appeal in the civilian federal court system, potentially delaying the execution for years, according to an article published in May in Army Lawyer.US military has not executed anyone since 1961Executions under the US military justice system are extremely rare. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on military death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.Former President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge later put the execution on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth.The last person executed by the US military was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old girl.Trump's approval of Hasan's execution comes days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order an independent review.Trump had previously resumed federal executions following an informal moratorium under earlier administrations. The federal government carried out 13 executions between 2020 and early 2021.Asked whether the failed Tennessee execution would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it “an interesting situation.”“It shouldn’t be very difficult,” Trump said of carrying out lethal injections.You use AI every day. articles.body: Israel was prepared to shoot down flydubai passenger jet carrying more than 150 Israelis after its captain was attacked in the cockpit and the aircraft plunged thousands of feet, CBS News reported, citing two Israeli sources with direct knowledge of the situation.According to the sources cited by CBS, Israel activated a long-established protocol for a potential 9/11-style incident after the aircraft plunged about 14,000 feet. The Israeli air force attempted to contact the cockpit but received no response.A pre-established committee was convened, a command centre was set up, fighter jets were scrambled and Israeli airspace was closed.The jets were recalled after Israeli authorities saw the aircraft turning towards Saudi Arabia, around 400 miles from Israel. Saudi Arabia also scrambled fighter aircraft in response.CBS reported that had the flydubai flight continued towards Israel, Israeli fighter jets could have entered Jordanian airspace to intercept and visually assess the aircraft. Pilots would have attempted to establish contact with the cockpit and inspect the cabin for signs of panic or a hijacking.Under the Israeli protocol, if a passenger aircraft was determined to be hijacked, remained unresponsive by radio and continued towards Israel without making demands, the matter would be escalated to the defence minister and prime minister.The protocol allows for the aircraft to be "shot down", with the final decision resting with the prime minister, according to the sources.Israeli officials told CBS that the suspected attacker, identified by sources as Omani national Hamam al Hamami, allegedly told UAE investigators that he had planned the attack before joining Flydubai and intended to crash the plane at Ben Gurion Airport. An Israeli official also said he had previously travelled to Israel.An early Israeli assessment indicated that the attempted hijacking was likely a lone-wolf attack, though the investigation remains ongoing and other possibilities are still being examined.The Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was approaching Israel on September 30 when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to crash the aircraft. articles.title: 'Expel rapists': Cornell students stage anti-rape rally in support of 'Jane Doe'
articles.summary: Hundreds of Cornell University students, faculty members and community activists marched across the campus on Tuesday in support of a student known as
articles.body: Hundreds of Cornell University students, faculty members and community activists marched across the campus on Tuesday in support of a student known as “Jane Doe”, demanding greater accountability from the Ivy League university over its handling of her alleged gang rape.The protesters called for an independent inquiry into Cornell’s response, uniform minimum sanctions for sexual assault cases, independent hearings and better training for campus police. Some also demanded the resignation of university president Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators.Carrying purple ribbons and placards reading “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe”, demonstrators chanted “One struggle, one fight” and “No justice, no peace” as they marched to Cornell’s main administration building.“Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” news agency AP quoted student Athena Holloway saying. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang told demonstrators: “Rape should not be inevitable.”The protest followed a lawsuit filed last month by Jane Doe, who alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after becoming incapacitated. She named seven fraternity members, the fraternity chapter, a bar, her sorority and Cornell as defendants.Doe reported the alleged assault to Cornell police in November 2024. No criminal charges were filed at the time, though Cornell conducted its own investigation and later shut down the Chi Phi chapter. The university has said some students were expelled and others received suspensions or other disciplinary measures.The accused men have denied wrongdoing, with some telling Cornell investigators that the sexual activity was consensual, according to records cited by news organisations. Lawyers for two of the former students have denied that their clients participated in a sexual assault.The case has drawn renewed scrutiny after New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over a reopened criminal investigation. Hochul has also called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case.The university's administration has defended its response while acknowledging concerns raised by the allegations. In a video message on Saturday, Kotlikoff said Jane Doe's account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”He also reaffirmed support for an independent review and pledged to work towards “finding the answers our community deserves.”The rally came after Cornell’s administration building was damaged early Monday, with two glass panes broken and graffiti painted on the entryway. One message read, “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED,” news agency Reuters reported.Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said the university was investigating the damage, adding that “damaging property is not the answer” to the community's “frustration and strong emotions.”The controversy has also intensified online, with supporters using the hashtag #IamJaneDoe.ABC News reported Monday that Doe had recorded a phone call with one of the men she accused before approaching Cornell police. During the call, she challenged him over what she said had happened, telling him, “What y'all did would be classified as gang rape.”The investigation into the allegations remains ongoing.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amazon Web Services' Swami Sivasubramanian says that CEOs are no longer worried if AI will add value to their businesses, now they have a new 'fear'
articles.summary: The ‘Big AI Question’ seems to have changed.
articles.body: The ‘Big AI Question’ seems to have changed. Until 2025, the general artificial intelligence (AI) worry was if investment in the technology was really worth it and if it will add to the bottomline. The same has shifted in 2026, and now the key concern is how safe are AI Agents. Companies do not yet trust AI with important decisions. According to a report by GeekWire, this was the general consensus at the recent Madrona's IA40 Summit. The Madrona's IA40 Summit is the venture capital company's annual gathering of AI startups, investors and tech executives. Zico Kolter, the Carnegie Mellon professor who chairs the safety and security committee of OpenAI's board, said that as of now Companies do not yet trust AI with important decisions. According to Kolter, the ability to control AI systems has to keep pace with their capabilities, which might mean developing them more slowly than is possible.His view was shared by Amazon Web Services (AWS) Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies organization head Swami Sivasubramanian. AWS's top executives said that most CEOs and CTOs worry about whether an AI agent will always follow their company’s rules and regulations. Speaking at the Summit, Sivasubramanian said that nearly every CIO and CEO raises the same question about AI agents. “How do I know it is always going to obey all my rules and regulations?” he said. “This is a real concern.” He added that companies can keep the creativity of AI models by pairing them with separate systems that check a model’s work against the company’s rules and catch violations.Sivasubramanian said that one of the least appreciated parts of making AI agents work is getting them the right company data for the task. He pointed out that teams inside Amazon were showing him impressive AI agents they had built in two or three weeks. When he asked when the agents could be rolled out, he said that almost every team told him it still had to work out security, identity and monitoring.AWS in June announced a service for that purpose, called AWS Context, which maps the relationships in a company’s data for agents to use. Sivasubramanian said it’s meant to work across platforms and cloud providers, and he expects this kind of service to be a basic building block for the next 20 years, as cloud storage and databases were two decades ago.AI has boosted profits, but the jump is not substantialMcKinsey senior partner Lari Hamalainen reportedly said that about 40% of companies claim AI has increased their profits, but only 6% describe the increase as substantial. Even as AI becomes more and more capable, there’s still lots of work to do to close the gap between “the goals, the capabilities, and what we all are aspiring to do,” McIlwain said.Madrona’s closing slide at the Summit said that returns on AI are still early for most of the companies using it but look inevitable based on what the earliest adopters are seeing.You use AI every day. articles.title: As Elon Musk plans to shake up mobile industry, AT&T CEO John Stankey says that the economics and technical aspects of Starlink's plan don't line up
articles.summary: AT&T CEO John Stankey has cast doubt on Musk's plans to turn SpaceX's Starlink satellite network into a direct competitor to wireless carriers, arguing
articles.body: AT&T CEO John Stankey has cast doubt on Musk's plans to turn SpaceX's Starlink satellite network into a direct competitor to wireless carriers, arguing that the economics and technical realities behind the strategy do not add up. Speaking to Axios, Stankey described SpaceX's ambition of becoming a major challenger to traditional telecom companies as "not a viable strategy," even as Elon Musk and Gwynne Shotwell, president of SpaceX, have outlined plans to expand Starlink beyond satellite internet and into mobile services. Starlink aims to challenge telecom operatorsThe comments come as SpaceX seeks to leverage Starlink's growing satellite network to compete more directly with established telecom operators. Shotwell recently said she expects Starlink to win customers from traditional carriers, arguing that the company's service would be superior. The remarks rattled investors, with shares of major telecom firms including AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile reportedly falling after SpaceX highlighted its ambitions. According to SpaceX's public disclosures, Starlink had 12 million subscribers and a constellation of 10,200 satellites covering 167 countries as of June 30. The connectivity business accounted for 55% of SpaceX's revenue, making it the company's biggest revenue generator.AT&T's counter-bet: fiber over satelliteAT&T is leaning hard on fiber infrastructure to grow its internet business at a moment when AI is driving surging demand for connectivity. The company announced a $3 billion deal with Corning on Tuesday to expand that infrastructure, arguing fiber delivers speeds three times faster than satellite. Stankey was blunt about the comparison, telling Axios that nothing beats fiber, and that even if satellite technology performs at its absolute best over the next decade, it still won't be able to match what fiber delivers.Starlink's mobile ambitionsStarlink already competes with traditional telecom companies for home and business internet customers, and SpaceX has now started talking openly about a mobile business that would put it in direct competition with wireless carriers. Shotwell added fuel to that narrative in August, during SpaceX's first earnings call as a public company, predicting the company would win over a meaningful number of customers because its service would simply be better. That comment sent shares of AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile falling the following day.As of June 30, Starlink had 12 million subscribers and more than 10,200 satellites providing coverage across 167 countries. While SpaceX's rockets and AI work tend to dominate headlines, its connectivity business is actually its largest revenue driver, accounting for 55% of total sales.The cost problemBecoming a genuine fourth major US mobile carrier would require significantly more terrestrial infrastructure to match a traditional cellular network's capacity — a build-out one analyst estimated could cost SpaceX more than $100 billion. SpaceX's alternative: installing small cellular base stations alongside Starlink dishes at homes and businesses, adding ground-based capacity where satellite alone falls short, without building a sprawling cell tower network. Musk claims these stations could eventually deliver connectivity directly to phones with better and higher bandwidth than existing carriers offer.Why Stankey says the math doesn't workStankey argued that installing enough small stations to match a traditional network's capacity would cost roughly the same as building a full macro cellular network. He also flagged a regulatory hurdle: current law doesn't allow radiating cellular signals from someone's home without their permission, unless the law changes. If the approach were genuinely viable, he argued, AT&T would already be doing it on its own fiber network. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.Analysts remain skeptical tooBernstein analyst Madison Rezaei wrote that cell towers aren't going anywhere soon, even if Musk gets creative, citing technical hurdles extending satellite coverage indoors, limited brand awareness, and customer reluctance to switch carriers. She suggested Starlink Mobile could fill a meaningful gap in remote, rural, maritime, or disaster scenarios, but remains a long way from replacing terrestrial carrier networks. operators' brands. She said Starlink Mobile could prove valuable in rural, remote, maritime and disaster-response scenarios but remains "a long way" from replacing terrestrial cellular networks.Despite the scepticism, the growing confrontation between SpaceX and established telecom providers highlights how satellite-based connectivity is increasingly moving into territory historically dominated by mobile network operators. As both sides invest billions to shape the future of communications, the battle between fibre, cellular networks and satellite internet appears set to intensify.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jim Bakker, who built ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire, has died at 86
articles.summary: Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful “The PTL Club” TV show, only to lose it all ove...
articles.body:
Jim Bakker, who along with his first wife Tammy Faye built an evangelical empire around the hugely successful "The PTL Club" TV show, only to lose it all over a sex scandal and financial crimes, has died. He was 86.

Bakker died Monday, his second wife, Lori Bakker, said in a statement. His cause of death was not immediately clear.

"He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry," she said.

The pair lived near the Missouri entertainment town of Branson and filmed their TV show "The Jim Bakker Show" there since it launched in 2003. Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020.

But it was another evangelical program that made Jim and his first wife Tammy Faye Bakker cultural icons — so much so that they were often skewered in the 1980s and 1990s by late-night comedians and parodied on "Saturday Night Live." A theatrical movie on their lives, "The Eyes of Tammy Faye," was released in September 2021.

At its peak in the mid-1980s, the Bakkers' ministry included not only the TV show drawing up to 13 million nightly viewers but also the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina.

Bakker got his start as a traveling preacher

Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry — he preached, she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country visiting churches and tent revivals.

They caught the attention of televangelist Pat Robertson, and in 1965 launched a children's show on Robertson's Christian Broadcasting Network. By 1966, he was hosting "The 700 Club," a Christian talk show.

Bakker left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — PTL stands for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show.

When it hit its heyday in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers — and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers.

The show featured chats with guests and Christian entertainers. Bakker offered upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye — charismatic and always wearing her trademark heavy mascara — sang. Most episodes were taped at their sprawling complex just south of Charlotte, North Carolina.

The couple was so famous that they were often parodied by TV comedians for their lavish lifestyle and Tammy Faye's abundant makeup.

Sex scandal and financial crimes damage his empire

In March 1987, their empire began to crack when Bakker admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn. Bakker was forced to resign from his own empire, turning over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell.

Tammy Faye stuck by Bakker, often with tears running down her mascara, even as many saw his downfall as a fitting symbol of the greed and hypocrisy of the 1980s.

In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL's finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years.

At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand."

Their marriage crumbled and Tammy Faye divorced Bakker in 1992, just short of their 31st anniversary, while he was still in prison. She later married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner was convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995 and spent about two years in prison.

Tammy Faye died of colon cancer in 2007.

Bakker was released on parole in 1994. He married his second wife, Lori, in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later.

In June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic.

The lawsuit said Bakker and a guest made the cure claim during 11 episodes in February and March of 2020.

Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002.

Salter, a former Associated Press journalist, was the main author of this obituary.

articles.body: The United States is closely monitoring a suspected plague infection involving a laboratory worker in Russia amid concerns that the disease may have spread internally, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said, while stressing that Washington's information on the case is based on details provided by Russian officials.Rubio made the remarks while speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a European visit. He said the US was aware of the case through information provided by Russian officials and was closely watching the situation over concerns that the infection could have spread internally.Rubio said the information available to Washington indicated that a worker at a Russian laboratory had been infected and that there was concern the infection may have spread within the facility.“We don't - we know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided, which is it seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that could have spread, at least internally,” he said.Rubio also indicated that quarantine measures had been taken in connection with the incident, although he did not provide details about the number of people affected or whether any internal transmission had been confirmed.He noted that travel between the US and Russia was currently limited, but said an infection that escapes its initial setting could spread quickly. “There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously. But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” he said.The remarks came after a laboratory worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died following pneumonia of unknown origin, prompting quarantine and medical monitoring of her contacts. Russian authorities have not confirmed plague as the cause of death, although reports have raised the possibility of pneumonic plague.Reports also alleged that the worker may have been exposed to plague bacteria in a laboratory incident, but Russian authorities have denied evidence of an accident involving dangerous pathogens. Authorities have identified the known contacts and reported no new cases among institute staff.There is also no confirmation that the worker had pneumonic plague or that human-to-human transmission occurred.You use AI every day. articles.title: Third-generation Massachusetts farmer grows broccoli and sweet corn beneath 832 solar panels; his 2.2-acre agrivoltaic farm wins Farmer of the Year
articles.summary: On a stretch of farmland in Hadley, Massachusetts, broccoli, sweet corn and other crops have been grown beneath rows of solar panels.
articles.body: On a stretch of farmland in Hadley, Massachusetts, broccoli, sweet corn and other crops have been grown beneath rows of solar panels. Farmer Joe Czajkowski, whose family has farmed in the Pioneer Valley for three generations, hosts an 832-panel agrivoltaic array covering 2.2 acres of his more than 400-acre farm. The 445-kilowatt DC system was built by Hyperion Systems and completed in July 2023, although the array became operational in 2024. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards has named Czajkowski its 2026 Solar Farmer of the Year, with the awards ceremony scheduled for October 27 in Chicago. The awards say half the electricity generated by the array runs his farm operations, while the other half goes to 17 low-income households across western Massachusetts. The U.S. Department of Energy says the panels are mounted at a 10-foot elevation to allow enough sunlight to reach crops below. UMass research and project materials from Hyperion describe the tracking system and its changing clearance above the ground.Massachusetts agrivoltaics farm: how Czajkowski Farm in Hadley hosts 832 solar panels over croplandCzajkowski Farm covers more than 400 acres in the Pioneer Valley, and the 2.2-acre solar array occupies a small portion of that land. The project was developed through a partnership between Czajkowski and Hyperion Systems, a company specialising in dual-use solar. Hyperion's project information says the array has a capacity of 445 kilowatts DC and 375 kilowatts AC and consists of 832 modules mounted on single-axis trackers. The rows are spaced 26 feet from post to post, allowing farm equipment to operate between them. Czajkowski can continue using tractors and attachments for activities including subsoiling, tilling, harrowing, cultivating and spraying. The modules are 10 feet above the ground when horizontal, according to Hyperion. Because the system tracks the sun, the clearance changes as the panels tilt. The UMass research summary records a maximum tilt that brings the panels to about 7.75 feet above the ground. The array uses a north-south single-axis tracking system, with the modules following the sun from east to west. The UMass research records the system as completed in July 2023.The project was designed around the farm's existing agricultural operation. Czajkowski continues to prepare the soil, plant, cultivate and harvest crops beneath the array, while also using the land for a winter cover crop. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards says the project qualified for both the Massachusetts SMART Program's Low Income Community Solar standards and its Agricultural Solar Tariff Generation Unit standards. Half of the electricity generated goes toward the farm's operations, while the other half serves 17 low-income households in western Massachusetts.Crops under solar panels: broccoli and sweet corn grow beneath the arrayBroccoli was selected for a 2023 experiment examining how the agrivoltaic array affected the crop's growing conditions. The UMass research summary, titled Broccoli Production Under Agrivoltaic Solar Array in Hadley, MA, describes the work as first-year preliminary results. Researchers transplanted broccoli on August 18, 2023, and monitored three bed positions beneath the array: one under the leading panel, one between two panels and one near the back panel. They compared these positions with control plots. The study examined growing conditions and crop performance at the different positions beneath the array. The researchers found that the leading-panel position received less photosynthetically active radiation than the control, while the other two positions received similar light levels to the control. Air temperature, relative humidity and soil temperature were similar between the array and control areas. The researchers described the findings as a snapshot of how the panels modified the crop-level microclimate and said further time-series analysis was planned. One important detail is that the 2023 trial took place before the system was connected to the grid. The UMass report says the panels remained horizontal during that trial year, so those results describe the conditions during that specific experiment rather than the fully operational tracking configuration.The project has since expanded beyond broccoli. The 2026 North American Agrivoltaics Awards says Czajkowski has grown sweet corn, blueberries and shade tobacco beneath the panels and has also raised broiler chickens under the array. It says sweet corn grown beneath the panels is producing about 80% of the volume of open-field corn while maintaining matching quality. The awards page separately attributes the roughly 20% difference to fewer corn rows being planted rather than stunted growth. That result comes from this farm and should not be treated as a general yield figure for sweet corn grown under agrivoltaic systems elsewhere. The farm also supplies produce to institutional and retail customers, including UMass Amherst Dining Services, Springfield Public Schools, Trader Joe's and Whole Foods, according to Hyperion's project information. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards says an electric van charged from the array is used to transport produce to UMass Dining.Dual-use solar for farmers: how the array provides another source of farm incomeFor Czajkowski, reducing the farm's electricity costs was one reason he became interested in solar. American Farmland Trust reported that his average annual electricity bill was around $75,000 and that he became interested in solar as a way to decrease that cost. The organisation reported that, under the arrangement described in its November 2023 article, Czajkowski would receive a 17.5% discount on his monthly electricity bills as a subscriber, equivalent to about $13,125 a year based on the $75,000 annual bill. American Farmland Trust also reported that the parcel used for the project had previously grown almost exclusively onions and had experienced degraded soil. Czajkowski wanted to make the land more viable, while the agrivoltaic project provided another use for the acreage alongside continued agricultural production. The Department of Energy quoted him saying he receives payments for the electricity while also getting a discount on his electric bill. The exact lease-payment amount has not been publicly disclosed in the cited accounts. The percentage discount has been reported differently in different accounts. American Farmland Trust's November 2023 article described a 17.5% discount for the subscriber arrangement, while later reporting has cited a figure of about 15%. The reports do not explain the difference between the two figures.Czajkowski told the Department of Energy that the solar income could provide another layer of financial security as he gets older. He also discussed additional agrivoltaic projects as a way of helping keep the farm viable for the next generation. The Hadley project is part of a wider expansion of agrivoltaics in the United States. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory identified 566 U.S. agrivoltaic projects as of August 2024, with more than 10 gigawatts of combined capacity. The figure comes from research published when the laboratory was still known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), now the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The U.S. Department of Energy's Solar Futures Study projected that solar could require about 5.7 million acres of land by 2035, equivalent to roughly 0.3% of the contiguous United States. DOE has highlighted agrivoltaics as one approach to combining solar generation with continued agricultural use of land. Its research and funding programmes have also examined how solar installations can coexist with crops and livestock.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Punjab government will approach the Supreme Court to challenge the Punjab and Haryana high court’s order directing a CBI probe into the matter concerning three letters written by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to the Punjab Director General of Police (DGP), AAP said.The state government will file an appeal against the High Court’s order.The High Court had on Monday directed that the matter be handed over to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) after hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by advocate Nikhil Thamman. The petition was filed after the Punjab Police allegedly failed to register a case based on the ED’s letters.The ED had sought registration of an FIR against Rajbir Singh Ghumman, Officer on Special Duty (OSD) to Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, and certain other individuals over alleged corruption.During the hearing, Thamman also submitted that Punjab has not had a regular DGP for more than four years. The petition referred to the Supreme Court’s judgment in the Prakash Singh vs Union of India case and its directions on the appointment of a regular DGP from a panel recommended by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC).Meanwhile, Punjab Congress chief Pargat Singh alleged systemic corruption in the state administration and warned officials against aligning with the government following the High Court’s order to transfer the matter to the CBI.Speaking to ANI, Singh criticised the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), calling the party and its members a “sham” and alleging that even the office of Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann has come under scrutiny."This party was created by the BJP as their own B-team, but the idea was to make the laws so strict that no matter who the minister or senior official was, anyone involved in corruption would automatically end up in jail. articles.title: Race to save rare South West recordings before they vanish
articles.summary: Fragile archive recordings revealing lost accents, lives and local history are being saved online.
articles.body:
Hundreds of recordings capturing the voices, accents and memories of people across the South West are being rescued before fragile tapes deteriorate beyond repair.

Archivists say some are at risk of being lost forever as ageing cassette and reel-to-reel tapes begin to break down.

The Sounds of the South West project is digitising them, preserving everything from Cornish dialect and sea shanties to memories of salmon fishing on the River Severn.

"It's a living history and it's a glimpse into the past, which you often don't find so easy to get from a book," said Philip Walker, head of culture and creative industries at Bristol City Council.

The project is making rare archive recordings available online for the first time, with plans to share around 1,500 clips from collections stretching from Gloucestershire to Cornwall.

"What we'll have is an incredible picture of the region's stories," said Walker.

"Either it's people's local accents, or it's what happened in their local communities."

The team of five staff at Bristol City Council's archives already has around 8,000 separate items, of which around 3,000 have been digitised.

Making recordings available online to the public requires diligent work not only to re-record them onto a digital format but to trace the owners, interviewees and copyright holders.

And in some cases, it is a race against time.

Walker said: "These recordings and the formats on which they're recorded are very, very fragile.

"Tape degrades over time and there's only a short window of opportunity left before they disintegrate and we'll lose whatever's on them."

Many of the 100 or so recordings currently on the website contain voices and snippets of oral history.

In one, Cornishman Fred Cock, who was born in St Ives, in 1929 recalls words of Cornish dialect such as 'crant' meaning a joke, or 'clidgey' for sticky.

Another features fisherman Deryck Huby from Gloucestershire who remembers the techniques and culture of salmon fishing on the River Severn.

In another, Joan Hellings, born in 1921 in Penryn, Cornwall, talks about her childhood and the days she spent exploring the town.

Among those helping preserve the region's history is 95-year-old Bristol jazz musician John Berry, who donated dozens of cassette recordings containing interviews with local musicians dating from the 1960s to the 1990s.

He said: "I was very interested in how they got into it, how they learned."

The recordings, made on a portable tape recorder, give a rare insight into Bristol's music scene in the 20th century.

They discuss what it was like to play in local venues, how musicians found work and how they learned their instruments.

Berry added: "I think people should have the ability to explore the cultures which have developed in the city."

"It does enable people who might research [jazz] something to build on."

Berry himself used his collection of recorded interviews to write a PhD and a book on how people learn to become musicians.

One of his interviews was with Arthur Parkman, who ran a rock night at Bristol's Colston Hall in the early 1960s.

In the recording, Parkman laments the fact he turned down the chance to book a then-unknown band from Liverpool for £100.

The band, called The Beatles, went on to enjoy a successful career in music.

The current collection could take another three years to fully digitise, although Walker said archivists would still welcome approaches from people with historically significant recordings.

"Archives are always interested in what material is out there," he said.

"I would recommend people approach their local archives in the first instance and speak to them about whether it's of interest and relevance."

articles.title: Durham council developing AI to process use of AI in info requests
articles.summary: Durham Council says it is getting more freedom of information requests written with the help of AI.
articles.body:
A council is building AI tools to help it process freedom of information (FOI) requests that are increasingly being written by AI.

Durham County Council's corporate data and insight manager Kim Teasdale said more residents were using AI to send in FOIs, which were longer and more complex than those constructed without technological assistance.

This meant more time was required to deal with each request, said Teasdale, so the council was exploring the use of AI tools to streamline the process.

The software could involve identifying and grouping together similar requests and pointing officials to relevant council responses to previous FOIs, she said.

In a report the authority said it had received 1,258 FOIs in the 12 months from June 2025.

That was 225 fewer than the same period the year before, but the council said processing time had increased due to the complexity of the requests which it suggested was because many were being written using AI.

This had led to a drop in the proportion of FOIs the council responded to within the expected 20 working days.

The authority also said it was looking into the use of an AI redaction tool to save time removing details from subject access requests.

Teasdale claimed AI tools would allow officials to work more efficiently and consistently while maintaining accuracy and there would always be "human oversight" in the process.

articles.title: 'Creating anarchy to relaunch Rahul': BJP on Congress's Form 6 claims
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra on Tuesday accused Rahul Gandhi of misleading the public over Form 6.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra on Tuesday accused Rahul Gandhi of misleading the public over Form 6. He alleged that the Congress and INDIA bloc were attempting to undermine constitutional institutions amid their planned protest against the Election Commission.Patra said the Supreme Court had not declared Form 6 illegal and had only agreed to examine allegations concerning changes to the form. He also rejected Gandhi's claim of differences within the Election Commission over the issue, citing an ECI fact-check that said the Bihar SIR order was approved unanimously."Rahul Gandhi posted today regarding Form 6 after the hearing in the Supreme Court on the PIL. This is an attack on the Election Commission, but the second line mentions the BJP as well, so the BJP will respond to it. Rahul Gandhi has misled the public on two points," Patra said."First, he claimed that Form 6 was illegal and specifically mentioned the Bharatiya Janata Party in this context. But the court did not declare Form 6 illegal today. The court noted that the petition mentioned changes to Form 6, so the court said it would examine the matter. We had not consented to any such changes. If any change has indeed been made, it will only become clear after the notice is issued," he said."Even after that, when we read the detailed order and look at the Election Commission's press release... it becomes clear that the Commission had explicitly stated that there was no change in Form 6, and the Supreme Court had upheld the associated declaration. Therefore, there is no ambiguity here. When Rahul Gandhi claims that Form 6 was illegal and that the Supreme Court said so today, he is lying," Patra added.Patra also hit out at the Congress and INDIA bloc over their planned march to the Election Commission, alleging that the opposition was seeking to weaken democratic institutions to facilitate Gandhi's political rise."A sponsored attempt is being made by opposition parties, especially the Congress, as to how a change of power can be brought about in the country and Rahul Gandhi be made to sit in power just like that. For this, a blow to India's democracy and constitutional bodies is being hurled in a sponsored manner," he said."After failing multiple times, Congress leaders decided to establish anarchy in the country and attack institutions... Today again, they are trying to create anarchy and undermine democratic institutions by allegedly marching towards the Election Commission," Patra said.He alleged that the Congress had been attempting for years to "launch and relaunch Rahul Gandhi", and accused the opposition of attacking institutions after failing to do so through electoral politics.On the alleged dissent within the poll panel, Patra said the Election Commission had clarified that its order on the Special Intensive Revision in Bihar was issued with the unanimous approval of all commissioners."The fact-check states that the order regarding SIR in Bihar was issued with the unanimous approval of the Commission. Subsequently, the Supreme Court of India upheld this order in its decision. It was indeed a unanimous decision with no room for doubt," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘I have cherished every moment of it, but…’: What this Australian Senator said while holding her infant daughter in Parliament
articles.summary: When Australian senator Fatima Payman addressed Parliament with her infant daughter Alia in her arms, the moment was striking not simply because a baby
articles.body: When Australian senator Fatima Payman addressed Parliament with her infant daughter Alia in her arms, the moment was striking not simply because a baby was inside the parliamentary chamber. It was what Payman chose to talk about while holding her daughter: the physical recovery after childbirth, the exhaustion and mental load of parenting, and why asking for help should not be seen as a failure.“This is the best thing that has ever happened to me. I have cherished every moment of it,” Payman said. “But, and there's a big but, it's bl**dy tough.”Her words capture a part of early parenthood that can easily get lost beneath photographs of happy new parents, carefully arranged baby announcements and expectations of how grateful a mother should feel.Payman became a mother earlier this year. According to SBS News, her daughter Aliyah was born in May, and Payman returned to Canberra to work four months later. Her working days now involve caring for a newborn alongside parliamentary responsibilities, including feeds, nappy changes, playtime and expressing breast milk.But rather than presenting motherhood as something that simply needs to be managed alongside work, Payman spoke about what it can demand from a woman physically and emotionally.“We don't talk enough about the physical recovery,” she said. “And colleagues, let me tell you, my birthing journey was… tough.”“It really sucked,” Payman added, while expressing gratitude towards the midwives and nurses who cared for both her and her daughter.For many new parents, the arrival of a baby is accompanied by an assumption that the difficult part is over once the birth is over. Payman’s comments point to a different reality: childbirth can be followed by a period of physical recovery at a time when a parent is simultaneously adjusting to feeding, interrupted sleep, changing routines and the constant needs of a newborn.And then there is the part that cannot always be seen. “Then there's the mental load, the silent suffering many parents carry alone, too afraid to speak up, worried of people's judgment,” she said.That mental load can be difficult to explain because parenting often involves dozens of small decisions and responsibilities that do not necessarily look like work from the outside. A parent may be physically sitting with a baby while mentally keeping track of feeds, sleep, appointments, household responsibilities and what needs to happen next.Payman’s larger point was not that motherhood is unhappy. In fact, she began by saying the opposite: that becoming a mother was the best thing that had happened to her and that she had cherished every moment.The two realities, however, can exist together. A parent can love their child deeply and still feel exhausted. They can be grateful and still need support. They can enjoy parts of parenting and struggle with others.Payman said she had decided not to hide that struggle.“Well, I'm not suffering in silence,” she said. “I'm asking for help. I'm talking to professionals, uh, because it's okay to get it wrong sometimes.” Her words also challenge the idea that parents are expected to know what they are doing from the moment their baby arrives. “It's okay to not be perfect, uh, or the perfect parent that society tells you to be,” Payman said, “because that parent doesn't exist.”For parents, that distinction can matter. The pressure to appear as though everything is under control can sometimes make it harder to acknowledge exhaustion or ask someone else to step in.Payman’s experience also comes in the context of returning to work while caring for a young baby. SBS News reported that she did not take an extended break from work after her daughter was born. She said she returned to work as soon as she could and began answering calls.Her circumstances have also highlighted wider questions around how workplaces accommodate parents. SBS reported that Australia's Parliament House has childcare facilities, parents' rooms and facilities for nursing and infant care, and that senators can breastfeed an infant in the chamber and, at the discretion of the Senate president, briefly care for an infant during proceedings as long as parliamentary business is not disrupted.But Payman’s message reaches beyond Parliament.Parenthood is often described through milestones - the first smile, the first steps, the first word. Less visible are the moments when a parent wonders whether they are doing enough, feels physically depleted or struggles to admit that they need another pair of hands.Payman ended her message with an idea that may be particularly reassuring to parents caught between love for their child and pressure to get everything right.“What exists is love done imperfectly and often held by the people around us, and that's enough.”For parents, perhaps that is the part worth remembering. There may never be a version of motherhood or fatherhood in which everything is perfectly managed. There may be difficult days alongside wonderful ones, uncertainty alongside confidence and moments when asking for help is the most responsible thing a parent can do.The perfect parent, as Payman put it, does not exist. What does exist is a parent trying, loving and sometimes leaning on the people around them.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ testGet the latest Lifestyle News and more. articles.title: How US ally South Korea is becoming a key fuel lifeline for Russia
articles.summary: US ally South Korea has emerged as a weak link in western sanctions against Russia, with more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel shipped from its ports to Russia
articles.body: US ally South Korea has emerged as a weak link in western sanctions against Russia, with more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel shipped from its ports to Russia in July and August, including cargoes carried by vessels sanctioned by the UK and EU, a Guardian investigation has found.The shipments included fuel carried by seven tankers on 14 voyages to Russia’s far east, with three of the vessels already under UK or EU sanctions.The Guardian’s analysis of South Korean port records and ship tracking data also found cases where tankers declared destinations such as Japan before sailing to Russia, while another sanctioned vessel received fuel through a ship-to-ship transfer near South Korea.Western sanctions on RussianWestern powers have targeted Russia’s oil trade to choke off a key source of revenue for Moscow’s war in Ukraine. The European Union bans imports of Russian seaborne crude and has also restricted imports of Russian petroleum products, while the G7-led price cap system limits access to western shipping and other maritime services for Russian oil sold above the permitted price.The EU has also stepped up efforts to target vessels involved in sanctions evasion. Its latest measures include port-access and service bans on additional vessels linked to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, as well as measures aimed at identifying ships and entities using deceptive practices to move Russian oil.Why Russia is importing fuelRussia is being forced to import refined fuel as Ukrainian drone strikes cripple its oil-refining capacity.According to The Guardian, Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, while diesel production dropped nearly 30 percent from a year earlier, forcing Moscow to look abroad for supplies.The scale of the shift is striking. Russia imports only small quantities of refined petroleum products, but in August it imported 368,000 tonnes by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.India was the largest supplier, while South Korea supplied 112,000 tonnes, accounting for 31 percent of Russia’s seaborne petroleum-product imports that month.You use AI every day. articles.title: No missiles, no bullets: US picks 4 new laser, microwave weapons to destroy drone swarms at the speed of light
articles.summary: The United States has selected four advanced laser and high powered microwave weapon systems for operational testing as Washington seeks to strengthen its
articles.body: The United States has selected four advanced laser and high powered microwave weapon systems for operational testing as Washington seeks to strengthen its defences against the growing threat posed by drones to military installations and critical infrastructure.According to the US Department of War, the systems will be evaluated under a directed energy pilot programme led by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, which is tasked with developing and coordinating counter drone capabilities for homeland defence.The move marks a shift towards testing directed energy weapons in operational environments rather than relying solely on conventional interceptors.The four systems selected for the pilot programme include AeroVironment’s Palletised High Energy Laser, Epirus’ Leonidas High Powered Microwave system, Kord’s Firefly High Energy Laser and Boeing’s Compact Laser Weapon System.The systems represent two major forms of directed energy technology being explored by the US military to counter unmanned aerial systems.How laser and microwave weapons workHigh energy laser weapons use concentrated electromagnetic energy to engage drones. The beam is focused on a specific part of the aircraft, delivering enough heat to damage critical components and potentially destroy the target.The US Army has described directed energy as offering a potentially lower cost per shot and a deeper magazine than conventional kinetic interceptors.Lasers also operate at the speed of light and do not require conventional ammunition, but their effectiveness depends on maintaining the beam on the target and can be affected by atmospheric conditions and other factors.High powered microwave(HPM) weapons work differently, using electromagnetic energy to interact with a drone's electronics. The US Office of Naval Research says HPM systems are designed to cause damage or temporary disruption to electronic systems, while their broader beams can allow multiple electronic targets to be engaged simultaneously.The US Army has tested HPM systems specifically designed to disrupt, disable or destroy multiple unmanned aircraft, making them a complementary layer alongside lasers and conventional counter drone weapons.

articles.title: Student union polls back in Odisha, education priority unchanged: Suryabanshi Suraj
articles.summary: Odisha to hold student union elections after 8-year gap; Higher Education Minister Suraj says process will be digitised via HIMS, with strict anti-violence rules.
articles.body: How did the govt decide this was the right time to hold student union elections?Reviving student union elections was one of our manifesto commitments. However, when the govt took office in 2024, it had to address several legacy issues. Many state universities were functioning without regular vice-chancellors, while the Odisha Universities (Amendment) Act, 2020, was under challenge in Supreme Court. The assembly amended the Act in April 2025, helping resolve the legal and administrative uncertainties. This year, we believe the system is fully prepared.Will parts of the election process be digitised?Much of university administration has already been digitised through the Higher Education Management System (HIMS), and the election process will also be integrated into it. Candidates will have to register on the HIMS portal. Digitised student data available through the Student Academic Management System will help identify eligible voters and candidates. Nomination filing, scrutiny and publication of valid nominations will be conducted online. Guidelines have also been issued for campaigning on social media, which will be closely monitored.Are colleges and universities prepared?We deliberately avoided announcing the elections too far in advance because a prolonged election period can affect the academic atmosphere. Once elections are announced, campus dynamics naturally change. The schedule has been designed to ensure that the process does not disrupt academic activities. The time available to institutions is in line with established norms and past practice.How will the govt prevent violence and politicisation?The elections will be conducted strictly in accordance with the Lyngdoh Committee guidelines. Authorities will maintain strict oversight over campaign expenditure and the use of banners and posters. The entry of outsiders into campuses will be prohibited, and police assistance will be taken wherever necessary. The expenditure limit for each candidate has been fixed at Rs 5,000. Candidates must submit detailed accounts through the HIMS portal within two weeks of the election. Political party slogans and hate speech will not be permitted. All banners and posters must be removed within 48 hours of the conclusion of the election process. Failure to do so will attract a penalty of Rs 1,500 per banner.How will political interference be checked?Political parties must recognise that these are student elections. The focus should remain on students and campus concerns, while sensitising young people to democratic processes and leadership.What assurance can you give parents concerned about academics?The entire process has been designed to conclude within two weeks. The short campaign period will limit disruption to academic activities and reduce the chances of violence.What are the govt’s other priorities?The govt is filling 1,435 teaching and non-teaching posts in universities, while the Odisha Public Service Commission will recruit more than 300 college teachers. articles.summary: More than two months after scores of box turtles were found abandoned along a riverbank in Cranford, New Jersey, the rescue effort has entered a new phase.
articles.body: More than two months after scores of box turtles were found abandoned along a riverbank in Cranford, New Jersey, the rescue effort has entered a new phase. The Mercer County Wildlife Center now reports caring for 219 turtles connected to the July dumping, up from about 190 in early August. With colder weather approaching, the centre is building two outdoor enclosures where many of the turtles will be able to spend the winter following the same seasonal cycle they would experience in the wild. Staff have nicknamed the new habitats Brumation Stations, a reference to the reptile equivalent of hibernation. Read on to know more:A riverbank littered with turtlesThe unusual rehabilitation effort began on July 29, when a Cranford resident discovered dozens of turtles abandoned along a riverbank near Riverside Drive and Casino Avenue, adjacent to the Rahway River. New Jersey Fish and Wildlife officers responded, and turtles began arriving at the Mercer County Wildlife Center in Hopewell Township and later at its River Road facility in Titusville. Residents were asked to bring any turtles they found to the Cranford Fire Department for safe transport to licensed rehabilitators, as per reports by News12 New Jersey and Abc7ny.com.The group included Eastern box turtles, which are native to New Jersey, and three-toed box turtles, a species not native to the state. Authorities have said the turtles were illegally dumped and that a law enforcement investigation is underway, but they have not announced who may have released them. Some investigators have examined whether the turtles were part of an illegal wildlife trade before being abandoned in the area. By mid-August, more than 200 box turtles had been recovered, and the Cranford Fire Department stopped accepting new turtles as the collection effort wound down. Recovered turtles were transported daily to the Mercer County Wildlife Center for treatment and evaluation. State wildlife officials said healthy Eastern box turtles would eventually be released into suitable habitat, while three-toed box turtles would be returned to wildlife agencies within their native range, as per the reports.Caring for hundreds of reptilesThe surge in patients put significant pressure on the Mercer County Wildlife Center, one of only three wildlife rehabilitation facilities in New Jersey permitted to care for reptiles. To handle the influx, staff and volunteers converted an entire building into temporary housing for the turtles. Every turtle has been seen by a veterinarian and is receiving a full medical workup, including triage, weight checks, X-rays, photographs, veterinary assessments, housing and feeding.Wildlife Center Director Jane Rakos-Yates said, according to The Cool Down (TCD), that each turtle requires dedicated enclosures, UV lighting, specific food and veterinary treatment, and those needs can become expensive quickly. The centre has asked supporters not to bring random produce, worms or aquariums, because the animals require very specific care. Instead, those looking to help are being encouraged to donate money or buy requested supplies through Wildlife Center Friends, the centre’s nonprofit partner.Rehabilitation manager Nicole Golden described the work as a community effort that has brought together state Fish and Wildlife officers and biologists, residents and firefighters from Cranford, local animal control officers, staffers and volunteers at the wildlife centre, the Mercer County Park Commission, veterinary specialists and members of the public, as per TCD. That broad collaboration has been essential in managing one of the biggest reptile rehabilitation efforts in the centre’s history.Preparing for winter with Brumation StationsAs autumn approaches, the focus has shifted to helping the turtles through the colder months. For healthy turtles, allowing them to follow their natural seasonal cycle is an important part of rehabilitation and can help prepare them for eventual release back into the wild, the Wildlife Center wrote in its October 3 update. With that goal in mind, the centre is constructing two outdoor enclosures where many of the turtles will be able to brumate, the reptile version of hibernation.The Brumation Stations are being built with assistance from the Mercer County Park Commission and supplies purchased with donations. The enclosures are designed to mimic the conditions the turtles would experience in the wild, with appropriate soil, shelter and protection from predators. The centre hopes to begin moving turtles into the new enclosures as early as this week, giving them time to settle in before the deepest cold sets in.Allowing the turtles to brumate outdoors serves both medical and behavioural purposes. It helps them maintain natural rhythms, supports their immune systems and reduces the stress of being kept indoors under artificial conditions for months. For a species that normally spends winter buried in leaf litter or soil, the chance to follow that pattern can improve their chances of survival after release.The road to releaseThe long-term goal remains rehabilitation and, when possible, returning turtles to the wild. State wildlife officials have said that healthy Eastern box turtles will be released into suitable habitat after veterinary evaluations, while three-toed box turtles will be returned to wildlife agencies within their native range. That process will take time, as each turtle must be assessed for health, weight, shell condition and overall fitness before it can be considered for release.For now, the turtles remain at the Mercer County Wildlife Center, where staff continue to monitor their health and prepare them for winter. The needs of 219 turtles are ongoing, and donations help provide food, supplies, veterinary care and everything needed to keep them healthy through the colder months. The centre’s update emphasised that public support remains critical as the rehabilitation effort moves into its next phase.A community rallying around wildlifeThe Cranford turtle dumping has drawn attention far beyond the immediate rescue. It has highlighted the challenges wildlife rehabilitators face when confronted with large-scale illegal releases and the importance of having licensed facilities equipped to handle such incidents. The case has also underscored the role of local residents, firefighters and animal control officers in identifying and reporting abandoned animals before they suffer further harm.For neighbours along the Rahway River, the sight of hundreds of turtles scattered along the bank was both alarming and heartbreaking. Many residents stepped forward to help, searching for turtles, bringing them to collection points and supporting the wildlife centre through donations and supplies. That community response has been a bright spot in an otherwise troubling episode, showing how quickly people can mobilise when local wildlife is at risk.As the Brumation Stations take shape, the focus is shifting from emergency rescue to long-term care and eventual release. For the 219 box turtles now in human hands, the hope is that they will one day return to a safe, natural habitat where they can live out their lives as wild animals. Until then, the Mercer County Wildlife Center and its partners will continue to provide the care and protection these reptiles need to survive.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
